For program [RESEARCH_PROGRAM], field [FIELD], metrics [CURRENT_METRICS], goals [CAREER_GOALS], timeline [TIMELINE], develop: bibliometric baseline and trajectory analysis, highest-leverage visibility activities for your career stage, review article and meta-analysis opportunity identification (most cited in your area by reviews), strategic collaboration network analysis to expand dissemination reach, conference and invited talk strategy for work-in-progress visibility, responsible citation practices building authentic community relationships, Google Scholar and ORCID optimization, and a two-year impact-building calendar.

prompts.title: Academic Book and Monograph Development Advisor
prompts.useCase: Transform a dissertation into a publishable book manuscript and navigate the academic book proposal and publication process
prompts.frameworks: Dissertation-to-book transformation (reframing, rewriting, not reformatting); Academic book proposal anatomy; Press selection matrix; Peer review process for books; Advance contract negotiation; Series vs standalone placement
prompts.output: Dissertation-to-book transformation plan with reframing strategy, book proposal structure, press selection rationale, and publication timeline
prompts.tip: A dissertation-to-book conversion is a fundamental reconceptualisation, not a surface edit. The dissertation was written for your committee; the book must be written for your entire field. Ask: what does someone outside my committee need to know to care about this argument?
prompts.prompt: You are an Academic Book and Monograph Development Advisor. For dissertation [DISSERTATION], presses [TARGET_PRESSES], field [FIELD], audience [AUDIENCE], timeline [TIMELINE], develop: dissertation-to-book transformation analysis identifying what must change (argument scope, literature framing, chapter structure, voice), book proposal anatomy with overview, chapter summaries, market analysis, and author qualifications sections, press selection matrix balancing prestige, fit, reach, and review timeline, advance contract considerations and what is and is not negotiable for first-time authors, peer review management strategy, and a 24-month timeline from dissertation to submitted manuscript.

prompts.title: Predatory Journal Detection and Publication Ethics Advisor
prompts.useCase: Protect your scholarly reputation by identifying predatory journals and navigating complex publication ethics situations
prompts.frameworks: COPE guidelines; Beall's criteria for predatory publishers; Think Check Submit; ICMJE authorship criteria; Duplicate publication and self-plagiarism; Image manipulation ethics; Data fabrication recognition
prompts.output: Publication ethics guidance with journal legitimacy checklist, authorship criteria application, data ethics guidelines, and escalation procedures for suspected misconduct
prompts.tip: When in doubt about a journal invitation, apply the Think Check Submit protocol — it takes five minutes and has saved many careers from the reputational damage of publishing in a predatory venue. No legitimate journal charges fees before peer review.
prompts.prompt: You are a Predatory Journal Detection and Publication Ethics Advisor. For invitation [JOURNAL_INVITATION], context [PUBLICATION_CONTEXT], stage [CAREER_STAGE], question [ETHICAL_QUESTION], field [FIELD], develop: journal legitimacy checklist using Think Check Submit, Beall's criteria, and indexing verification, authorship criteria application using ICMJE guidelines for your specific authorship situation, guidance on ghost writing, gift authorship, and corresponding author responsibilities, self-plagiarism and duplicate publication boundaries and how to avoid them, data and image ethics with specific red-line rules, complaint and escalation procedures if you witness misconduct, and institutional resources available to you for ethics consultation.

s28.label: Research Collaboration, Supervision, and Lab Culture

prompts.title: Advisor and Committee Relationship Strategist
prompts.useCase: Navigate the most important professional relationship in your PhD — the advisor relationship — with sophistication and self-advocacy
prompts.frameworks: Advisor-advisee relationship typology; Meeting management; Feedback reception and negotiation; Expectation alignment; Co-authorship negotiation; Difficult conversation frameworks applied to power-asymmetric relationships
prompts.output: Advisor relationship strategy with communication structure, meeting protocol, feedback management, expectation alignment plan, and escalation pathway for serious dysfunction
prompts.tip: Your advisor cannot manage a relationship they cannot see. Make your work, your progress, and your challenges visible through structured communication — weekly email updates, documented meeting notes, and explicit milestone discussions. Advisors who seem disengaged often simply do not know enough about your situation to engage.
prompts.prompt: You are an Advisor and Committee Relationship Strategist. For style [ADVISOR_STYLE], challenges [RELATIONSHIP_CHALLENGES], stage [DISSERTATION_STAGE], patterns [COMMUNICATION_PATTERNS], goals [GOALS], develop: communication structure making your progress and needs visible, meeting protocol with agenda template and documentation practice, feedback reception and negotiation strategy for unhelpful or contradictory feedback, expectation alignment conversation guide for scope, timeline, and co-authorship, individual committee member relationship management plan, escalation pathway if the advisor relationship becomes seriously dysfunctional, and self-advocacy scripts for common difficult conversations (requesting more feedback, negotiating timeline, raising mental health concerns).

prompts.title: Research Collaboration and Co-Authorship Manager
prompts.useCase: Structure, manage, and protect your contributions in multi-author research collaborations
prompts.frameworks: ICMJE authorship criteria; Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT); Collaboration agreement design; Co-authorship order conventions by field; IP and data ownership; Cross-institutional collaboration governance
prompts.output: Collaboration management framework with contribution tracking, authorship agreement template, communication protocols, conflict resolution procedure, and data management plan
prompts.tip: Authorship disputes are among the most damaging conflicts in academic careers. Establish authorship order and contribution expectations in writing before the project begins — a brief email thread confirming what was agreed is better than nothing.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Collaboration and Co-Authorship Manager. For type [COLLABORATION_TYPE], collaborators [COLLABORATORS], contributions [CONTRIBUTION_ALLOCATION], field [FIELD], history [CONFLICT_HISTORY], develop: contribution tracking system using CRediT taxonomy, collaboration agreement template covering authorship, data ownership, IP, publication rights, and withdrawal procedures, authorship order conventions for your field and how to negotiate them, communication and project management protocols for distributed teams, conflict escalation procedure for authorship disputes, cross-institutional collaboration agreement considerations, and data sharing and management plan meeting funder requirements.

prompts.title: PhD Mental Health and Wellbeing Protection Guide
prompts.useCase: Proactively protect your mental health throughout the PhD with evidence-based strategies and early intervention
prompts.frameworks: PhD mental health research (Levecque 2017); Maslach Burnout Inventory adapted for PhD; Identity disruption and imposter syndrome; Isolation reduction; Help-seeking in academic culture; Crisis resource navigation
prompts.output: Personalised PhD wellbeing plan with early-warning system, social infrastructure design, institutional resource map, crisis prevention protocol, and sustainable productivity practices
prompts.tip: The PhD mental health crisis is structural, not personal — rates of depression and anxiety among PhD students are six times higher than in the general population. Struggling is normal and expected; struggling in silence is the dangerous choice. Build your support infrastructure before you need it.
prompts.prompt: You are a PhD Mental Health and Wellbeing Protection Guide. For stage [PhD_STAGE], stressors [CURRENT_STRESSORS], network [SUPPORT_NETWORK], institution [INSTITUTION], risks [RISK_FACTORS], develop: PhD-specific mental health risk assessment with your personal risk factor profile, early-warning indicator system for your specific patterns, social infrastructure design countering academic isolation, institutional resource mapping (counselling, student services, ombudsperson, graduate student unions), academic culture navigation for help-seeking without career risk, sustainable productivity practices preventing burnout, and crisis resources and escalation plan if early intervention is needed.

prompts.title: Research Group and Lab Dynamics Navigator
prompts.useCase: Thrive in your research group environment — navigating lab culture, peer relationships, and resource competition
prompts.frameworks: Lab culture typology; Peer collaboration vs competition; Resource access negotiation; Intellectual property within groups; Lab meeting dynamics; Senior-junior student relationships; Exit strategies for toxic lab environments
prompts.output: Lab navigation strategy with relationship mapping, resource access approach, meeting participation strategy, peer collaboration design, and escalation path for toxic dynamics
prompts.tip: Every lab has informal rules that are more important than formal ones. In your first three months, observe more than you participate — identify who has informal influence, how resources actually get allocated, and what behaviours the PI actually rewards versus what they say they value.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Group and Lab Dynamics Navigator. For structure [LAB_STRUCTURE], PI style [PI_STYLE], peer dynamics [PEER_DYNAMICS], resources [RESOURCES], challenges [CHALLENGES], develop: lab culture mapping identifying formal and informal power structures, resource access strategy for equipment, funding, and PI time, meeting participation approach maximising your visibility and contribution, peer collaboration design for mutual benefit without naive information sharing, senior-junior student relationship cultivation, intellectual property clarity within your group, and an exit strategy assessment for lab environments that become untenable.

prompts.title: International and Cross-Cultural Research Partnership Architect
prompts.useCase: Build and manage productive international research collaborations across cultural, institutional, and linguistic differences
prompts.frameworks: Cross-cultural research ethics; Data sovereignty; Authorship in global south partnerships; Communication across time zones; Research collaboration agreements; Decolonising research partnerships; GDPR and cross-border data transfer
prompts.output: International collaboration framework with cultural communication guide, agreement structure, data management across jurisdictions, ethical partnership principles, and virtual collaboration management
prompts.tip: Power asymmetries in international collaborations are real and consequential. If you are the researcher from the well-resourced institution, actively work to ensure your partners' intellectual contributions are recognised in authorship, funding, and credit — research partnerships built on extraction eventually collapse.
prompts.prompt: You are an International and Cross-Cultural Research Partnership Architect. For partners [PARTNER_INSTITUTIONS], cultural contexts [CULTURAL_CONTEXTS], goals [RESEARCH_GOALS], funding [FUNDING], tools [COMMUNICATION_TOOLS], develop: cross-cultural communication guide for your specific partnership contexts, research collaboration agreement adapted for international contexts, data sovereignty and cross-border data transfer compliance, authorship and IP equity considerations in asymmetric partnerships, ethics review coordination across different national IRB equivalents, virtual collaboration management across time zones and languages, decolonising research practice principles for your specific context, and funding strategy for sustaining international partnerships beyond initial grants.

s29.label: Postdoctoral Research and Academic Job Market

prompts.title: Academic Job Market Application Architect
prompts.useCase: Build a complete, compelling academic job application package that survives initial screening and wins interview invitations
prompts.frameworks: Academic job application components (cover letter, research statement, teaching statement, diversity statement, CV); Search committee psychology; Screening vs selection criteria; Tailoring strategy; Academic job market timeline
prompts.output: Complete academic application strategy with document templates, tailoring framework, screening survival analysis, and application calendar
prompts.tip: Your cover letter's opening paragraph is screened by a committee that has read 200 similar letters that day. Do not begin with 'I am writing to apply for...' Begin with your most compelling scholarly sentence — the thing that makes your work sound alive and necessary.
prompts.prompt: You are an Academic Job Market Application Architect. For field [FIELD], stage [CAREER_STAGE], positions [TARGET_POSITIONS], qualifications [QUALIFICATIONS], context [MARKET_CONTEXT], develop: cover letter structure with compelling opening, research identity statement, teaching philosophy integration, and institutional fit argument, research statement architecture for your career stage (dissertation-complete vs postdoc), teaching statement framework with concrete evidence of effectiveness, diversity statement that is substantive rather than performative, CV structure and curation strategy for maximum impact, tailoring framework for R1 vs teaching-focused vs liberal arts vs international positions, and a screening-survival analysis identifying the filters your application must pass.

prompts.title: Academic Job Talk and Campus Visit Performance Coach
prompts.useCase: Deliver a job talk that demonstrates your research excellence and makes every person in the room want to hire you
prompts.frameworks: Job talk architecture (broad hook, research program narrative, key findings, future directions, departmental fit); Dual audience management (specialists and generalists); Q&A management; Campus visit social navigation; Chalk talk (science) conventions
prompts.output: Complete job talk preparation plan with structure, opening strategy, findings presentation, future research vision, Q&A simulation, and campus visit social navigation guide
prompts.tip: Your job talk's opening five minutes must be accessible to every person in the room, including those outside your subfield. If specialists are the only ones engaged by your opening, generalists have already mentally moved to the next candidate. Earn the whole room before going deep.
prompts.prompt: You are an Academic Job Talk and Campus Visit Performance Coach. For research [RESEARCH], audience [AUDIENCE], format [TALK_FORMAT], field [FIELD], vulnerabilities [VULNERABILITIES], develop: talk structure for your specific format and field norms, opening that hooks both specialists and generalists, research program narrative showing a coherent intellectual identity beyond the dissertation, future directions that demonstrate funded research potential, findings presentation calibrated to a mixed disciplinary audience, chalk talk or teaching demonstration preparation if required, anticipated Q&A with model responses, campus visit social navigation (meals, informal meetings, student interactions), and post-visit communication strategy.

prompts.title: Postdoctoral Position Search and Selection Strategist
prompts.useCase: Identify, evaluate, and secure the postdoctoral position that best positions you for your target career
prompts.frameworks: Postdoc selection criteria matrix; Independence vs training trade-off; Fellowship vs staff postdoc distinction; Mentor evaluation framework; Postdoc-to-faculty transition planning; Industry and alt-ac postdoc options
prompts.output: Postdoc search strategy with opportunity identification, mentor evaluation framework, position comparison matrix, negotiation approach, and career development planning within the postdoc
prompts.tip: Choose your postdoc mentor as carefully as your PhD advisor. Visit for a full day, talk to their current and former postdocs privately, and ask explicitly: 'How many of your postdocs have gone on to the type of position I want?' Past results are better evidence than present promises.
prompts.prompt: You are a Postdoctoral Position Search and Selection Strategist. For goals [CAREER_GOALS], program [RESEARCH_PROGRAM], locations [PREFERRED_LOCATIONS], funding [FUNDING_OPTIONS], timeline [TIMELINE], develop: opportunity identification strategy (fellowship search, PI cold-contact approach, network referrals), mentor evaluation framework with red flag and green flag indicators, position comparison matrix weighing research freedom, publishing support, mentoring quality, and career launching resources, fellowship application strategy for independent postdoc funding, negotiation approach for salary, start-up, and career development commitments, career development planning within the postdoc maximising publication output and grant writing experience, and a two-year postdoc milestone plan targeting your specific next role.

prompts.title: Academic Tenure and Promotion Dossier Architect
prompts.useCase: Build a compelling tenure and promotion case that tells a coherent narrative of scholarly excellence
prompts.frameworks: Tenure dossier components; Personal statement for tenure; Scholarship framing (teaching-focused vs research-focused institutions); External letter strategy; Evidence curation and narration; Pre-tenure review as dry run
prompts.output: Tenure dossier strategy with personal statement narrative, evidence curation approach, external reviewer selection, documentation best practices, and timeline for pre-tenure review
prompts.tip: Your tenure personal statement is not a CV summary — it is a scholarly autobiography that makes the case that your work constitutes a coherent, significant, and ongoing contribution to your field. Write it as if explaining your intellectual life to a brilliant colleague in a different field.
prompts.prompt: You are an Academic Tenure and Promotion Dossier Architect. For stage [CAREER_STAGE], institution [INSTITUTION_TYPE], research [RESEARCH_RECORD], teaching [TEACHING_RECORD], service [SERVICE_RECORD], develop: personal statement narrative connecting your research, teaching, and service into a coherent scholarly identity, research record framing with contribution claims beyond the publication list, teaching portfolio curation with evidence of effectiveness and innovation, service record contextualisation showing departmental citizenship, external reviewer selection strategy (criteria, identification, and approach), documentation systems for ongoing dossier building, pre-tenure review strategy to identify and address weaknesses early, and institution-specific standard interpretation for your policies.

prompts.title: Alt-Academic and Non-Academic Career Transition Coach for PhDs
prompts.useCase: Translate your doctoral skills and knowledge into compelling candidacy for careers beyond the tenure track
prompts.frameworks: Transferable skills articulation; Alt-ac career typology (policy, industry research, consulting, nonprofit, government, tech); Skills-to-role mapping; Narrative translation for non-academic audiences; Network building outside academia
prompts.output: Alt-academic career transition strategy with skills translation, sector-specific narrative, job search approach, network building plan, and application material adaptation
prompts.tip: The biggest barrier to alt-ac career transitions is not skills — it is the inability to translate what you did in academic language into what employers outside academia value. 'Conducted six years of qualitative fieldwork' becomes 'led a multi-year stakeholder engagement programme generating deep organisational insight.'
prompts.prompt: You are an Alt-Academic and Non-Academic Career Transition Coach for PhDs. For field [PhD_FIELD], target [TARGET_SECTOR], skills [TRANSFERABLE_SKILLS], constraints [CONSTRAINTS], timeline [TIMELINE], develop: doctoral skills audit mapping PhD experience to non-academic competency frameworks, narrative translation guide converting academic language to professional language for each skill, sector-specific career pathway analysis for your target sector, job search strategy including LinkedIn optimisation, informational interview approach, and application tailoring, network building plan in your target sector from zero, cover letter and resume (not CV) conversion strategy, and a timeline with concrete milestones from decision to employed.

prompts.title: Research Program and Scholarly Identity Architecture Guide
prompts.useCase: Build a coherent, distinctive, and fundable long-term research program identity beyond the dissertation
prompts.frameworks: Research program design; Scholarly identity construction; Intellectual agenda setting; Research question pipeline; Programmatic grant strategy (R01, ERC, AHRC programme grants); Niche vs broad research identity trade-offs
prompts.output: Long-term research program design with core identity statement, question pipeline, funding strategy, publication agenda, and five-year scholarly vision
prompts.tip: Your research program is not a list of projects — it is a coherent answer to the question: what am I the scholar who studies? Define your intellectual territory with enough specificity to be distinctive and enough breadth to sustain a career. The best scholarly identities fit in one sentence.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Program and Scholarly Identity Architecture Guide. For dissertation [DISSERTATION_TOPIC], questions [FUTURE_QUESTIONS], field [FIELD], stage [CAREER_STAGE], funding [FUNDING_LANDSCAPE], develop: core research program identity statement in one to two sentences, intellectual territory map showing the questions, phenomena, and theoretical debates you own, research question pipeline organised into short (dissertation, postdoc), medium (early career), and long-term (mid-career) horizons, funding strategy aligning your questions to available mechanisms, publication agenda connecting your questions to high-impact venues, and a five-year scholarly vision statement you can use in job talks, grant proposals, and promotion reviews.

prompts.title: Research Report Architect
prompts.useCase: Structure and write comprehensive research reports for any audience — academic, policy, or practitioner
prompts.frameworks: IMRaD structure; Executive Summary writing; Audience analysis (Covino & Jolliffe); Plain language principles; Technical writing ladder (Weiss); Evidence hierarchy presentation
prompts.output: Fully structured report outline with section-by-section writing guidance, executive summary template, key findings narrative, audience-appropriate language calibration, and visual element placement recommendations
prompts.tip: Write the executive summary last — it should crystallise your key messages after you know exactly what your evidence supports, not before.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Report Architect specialising in multi-audience scientific communication. For research on [RESEARCH_TOPIC] targeting [AUDIENCE_TYPE], purpose [REPORT_PURPOSE], key findings [KEY_FINDINGS]: design a complete report structure with executive summary (problem-method-findings-recommendations format), methodology summary, findings narrative with evidence hierarchy, discussion of implications, recommendations with action prioritisation, and audience-calibrated language guide. Include advice on figures, tables, and data visualisation placement.

prompts.title: Research Findings Narrative Writer
prompts.useCase: Transform raw results and data tables into compelling, scholarly findings narratives
prompts.frameworks: Results-to-narrative translation; Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) model; Data-driven storytelling (Knaflic); Theme-first vs data-first organisation; Scholarly hedging language
prompts.output: Complete findings narrative with theme organisation, evidence integration, claim-evidence-reasoning chains, appropriate hedging and qualification language, and transition architecture between findings
prompts.tip: Separate 'what you found' from 'what it means' — mixing results and interpretation is the most common findings chapter error and the one reviewers flag most often.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Findings Narrative Specialist. For a [STUDY_TYPE] study with results [RAW_RESULTS], research questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], framework [THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK]: construct a scholarly findings narrative with organised theme structure, data-to-claim translation, evidence integration (tables, quotes, statistics woven into prose), appropriate epistemic hedging, inter-finding transitions, and distinction between descriptive results and interpretive commentary. Flag where visual elements (tables/figures) should break the prose.

prompts.title: Research Abstract and Summary Specialist
prompts.useCase: Write high-impact abstracts and plain-language summaries for journals, conferences, and public audiences
prompts.frameworks: Structured abstract (Background-Objective-Methods-Results-Conclusion); Unstructured abstract; ASSERT guidelines; Plain Language Summary (PLS) standards; 6-word summary technique
prompts.output: Multiple abstract versions (structured, unstructured, plain-language, social media), each calibrated to word limit with keyword optimisation advice and impact-maximising language choices
prompts.tip: Lead with your most significant finding in the abstract — not your background. Reviewers and search algorithms reward novelty and specificity in the opening sentence.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Abstract and Summary Specialist. For research summarised as [FULL_PAPER_SUMMARY], targeting [VENUE_TYPE], within [WORD_LIMIT] words, contribution [KEY_CONTRIBUTION]: write four versions — (1) structured abstract (BMRC format), (2) unstructured narrative abstract, (3) plain-language summary for non-expert audience, (4) 280-character social media summary. For each, explain language choices, highlight how the contribution is foregrounded, and provide keyword recommendations for database discoverability.

prompts.title: Research Discussion Chapter Strategist
prompts.useCase: Build rigorous, theoretically grounded discussion sections that connect findings to literature and generate knowledge claims
prompts.frameworks: Discussion chapter architecture (Swales & Feak); Establishing territory-niche-occupying (CARS model revisited); Confirmation-contradiction-extension typology; Alternative explanation testing; Limitation framing (strength vs weakness language)
prompts.output: Complete discussion architecture with finding-to-literature mapping, confirmation/extension/contradiction structure, theoretical contribution claims, alternative explanation analysis, limitation narrative, and implication hierarchy (theoretical, methodological, practical, policy)
prompts.tip: For each unexpected finding, present and refute at least two alternative explanations before asserting your preferred interpretation — this is what separates sophisticated discussion from descriptive summary.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Discussion Chapter Strategist. For findings [KEY_FINDINGS], literature context [EXISTING_LITERATURE], framework [THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK], unexpected results [UNEXPECTED_RESULTS]: design a complete discussion section with (1) findings-to-literature mapping (confirmation, extension, contradiction for each key finding), (2) theoretical contribution claims with appropriate epistemic confidence, (3) alternative explanation consideration and refutation, (4) limitation discussion (reframe as scope conditions where possible), (5) implication hierarchy across theoretical, methodological, practical and policy levels, (6) future research agenda with specific next-step questions.

prompts.title: Research Methods Section Writer
prompts.useCase: Write transparent, reproducible, and defensible methodology sections for any research design
prompts.frameworks: Transparency and reproducibility standards (TOP guidelines); CONSORT/STROBE/COREQ reporting checklists; Procedural transparency; Audit trail documentation; Ethical reporting standards
prompts.output: Complete methods section with research design justification, participant/sample description, data collection procedures, instrumentation description, analytical procedures, validity/reliability/rigour evidence, ethical considerations, and reproducibility checklist
prompts.tip: Write your methods as if a stranger must exactly replicate your study with only your text as guidance — if they couldn't, your methods section is not yet complete.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Methods Section Writing Specialist. For design [RESEARCH_DESIGN], procedures [DATA_COLLECTION_PROCEDURES], sample [SAMPLE_DESCRIPTION], analysis [ANALYSIS_APPROACH]: write a complete, reproducible methods section with: research design overview and epistemological justification, participant/sample description and selection rationale, data collection procedures (step-by-step), instrumentation and materials description, analytical procedures with software and decision trail, validity/reliability/rigour criteria appropriate to paradigm, ethical considerations and approvals, and a self-assessment checklist against the relevant reporting guideline (CONSORT/COREQ/STROBE).

prompts.title: Research Introduction and Background Writer
prompts.useCase: Craft compelling research introductions that establish significance, identify the gap, and justify the study
prompts.frameworks: CARS model (Swales): Establish Territory, Establish Niche, Occupy Niche; Funnel architecture; Problem-gap-hook structure; Significance argument typology (theoretical/practical/social); Rationale statement construction
prompts.output: Complete introduction with territory establishment, literature landscape summary, gap articulation, study rationale, purpose statement, research questions or hypotheses, and significance argument — with CARS move-by-move annotation
prompts.tip: Your gap statement must be specific enough that your study is the obvious solution — vague gaps invite the question 'but hasn't someone already done this?' Cite the absence of evidence as evidence of the gap.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Introduction Writing Specialist using the CARS model (Swales). For topic [RESEARCH_TOPIC], field context [FIELD_CONTEXT], gap [KNOWLEDGE_GAP], rationale [STUDY_RATIONALE]: write a complete introduction section with: Move 1 — territory establishment (field significance, prior research landscape), Move 2 — niche establishment (gap identification with citation of what is missing or contradictory, problem statement, significance argument), Move 3 — niche occupation (purpose statement, research questions or hypotheses, study overview, contribution preview). Annotate each CARS move explicitly for learning, then produce the clean version.

prompts.title: Research Conclusion and Implications Framer
prompts.useCase: Write definitive, impact-oriented conclusions that synthesise findings and articulate research contributions
prompts.frameworks: Conclusion architecture (synthesis vs summary distinction); Contribution typology (theoretical/methodological/empirical/practical/policy); Implication cascade; Call-to-action research agenda; Legacy argument construction
prompts.output: Complete conclusion section with findings synthesis (not summary), contribution statement by type, tiered implications for different stakeholder audiences, research agenda with specific future questions, and closing legacy argument
prompts.tip: A conclusion synthesises — it tells the reader what the findings mean together, not what each finding showed individually. If your conclusion reads like a list, rewrite it as an argument.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Conclusion Specialist. For study [STUDY_SUMMARY], findings [MAIN_FINDINGS], audiences [TARGET_AUDIENCES], contribution type [CONTRIBUTION_TYPE]: write a complete conclusion with: (1) synthesis statement (what the findings mean together, not individually), (2) contribution statement by category — theoretical advancement, methodological innovation, empirical addition, practical guidance, policy implication, (3) tiered implications for each target audience with specific action language, (4) research agenda: five specific future questions generated by this study's findings and limitations, (5) closing legacy argument — why this study matters for the field's trajectory.

prompts.title: Systematic Review Protocol Designer
prompts.useCase: Design PRISMA-compliant systematic review protocols with search strategies, eligibility criteria, and data extraction frameworks
prompts.frameworks: PRISMA 2020 checklist; PICO/PICOS/SPIDER frameworks; Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews; Preferred Reporting Items; Boolean search logic; Eligibility criteria design (Methley et al.)
prompts.output: Complete systematic review protocol with PICO elements, boolean search strings for each database, PRISMA-compliant flow diagram template, inclusion/exclusion criteria, data extraction form, quality appraisal tool selection, and synthesis plan
prompts.tip: Register your systematic review protocol in PROSPERO before you begin screening — retrospective registration is rejected, and pre-registration protects against accusations of outcome-driven exclusion decisions.
prompts.prompt: You are a Systematic Review Protocol Specialist. For review question [REVIEW_QUESTION], PICO elements [PICO_ELEMENTS], databases [DATABASES], criteria [INCLUSION_EXCLUSION_CRITERIA]: design a complete PRISMA 2020-compliant protocol with: (1) structured review question with all PICO components, (2) boolean search strings tailored to each database with MeSH/subject headings and free-text terms, (3) PRISMA flow diagram template (identification-screening-eligibility-inclusion stages), (4) explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria with decision rules for edge cases, (5) data extraction form template, (6) risk of bias appraisal tool recommendation (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, CASP, etc.) with rationale, (7) synthesis plan (meta-analysis vs narrative synthesis decision tree).

prompts.title: Scoping Review Architect
prompts.useCase: Design scoping reviews to map the extent and nature of evidence on a topic using Arksey & O'Malley and JBI frameworks
prompts.frameworks: Arksey and O'Malley (2005) framework; JBI Scoping Review Methodology; PRISMA-ScR extension; Concept-Context-Population (CCP); Charting framework design; Thematic mapping
prompts.output: Complete scoping review protocol with CCP framework, search strategy, inclusion/exclusion rationale, charting data form, thematic mapping plan, and PRISMA-ScR compliance checklist
prompts.tip: Scoping reviews map what exists — they should not grade evidence quality or make recommendations. If you find yourself evaluating study quality, you may have drifted into systematic review territory.
prompts.prompt: You are a Scoping Review Methodology Specialist using Arksey and O'Malley's framework enhanced by JBI guidance. For question [SCOPING_QUESTION], concept-population-context [CONCEPT_POPULATION_CONTEXT], evidence types [EVIDENCE_TYPES], charting needs [CHARTING_NEEDS]: design: (1) scoping question with explicit concept, population, and context boundaries, (2) comprehensive search strategy across sources (databases, grey literature, reference lists), (3) source selection criteria with rationale and edge-case decision rules, (4) data charting framework capturing key variables, (5) thematic mapping approach for synthesising the landscape, (6) PRISMA-ScR checklist compliance assessment, (7) plan for stakeholder consultation (if relevant), (8) guidance on distinguishing findings from recommendations.

prompts.title: Narrative and Thematic Literature Review Synthesiser
prompts.useCase: Construct analytically rigorous narrative literature reviews that synthesise, critique, and position research within a field
prompts.frameworks: Narrative synthesis (Popay et al.); Thematic literature review structure; Critical synthesis vs descriptive annotation; Literature clustering and gap mapping; Conceptual framework development from literature
prompts.output: Complete narrative review structure with thematic organisation, critical synthesis approach, conceptual gap map, literature clustering rationale, and a synthesised argument that positions the reviewer's own research
prompts.tip: A good literature review argues — it builds a case for why your study is needed. Every paragraph should advance that argument, not merely report what each author said.
prompts.prompt: You are a Narrative Literature Review Synthesis Specialist. For topic [REVIEW_TOPIC], purpose [REVIEW_PURPOSE], lens [THEORETICAL_LENS], scope [SCOPE_AND_BOUNDARIES]: design and partially draft a narrative review with: (1) thematic clustering strategy for organising the literature, (2) critical synthesis approach (agreement, contradiction, evolution of thought across studies), (3) conceptual gap map (what exists, what is contested, what is absent), (4) theoretical framework synthesis from the literature, (5) argument architecture — how the review builds the case for the target study, (6) sample synthesis paragraph demonstrating analytical (not descriptive) engagement with 3-4 sources, (7) common literature review errors to avoid (annotation error, recency bias, tunnel vision).

prompts.title: Research Gap Identification and Positioning Advisor
prompts.useCase: Identify genuine knowledge gaps in a field and position a study to fill them with scholarly precision
prompts.frameworks: Gap typology (empirical/theoretical/methodological/population/contextual); Niche positioning (CARS model); Lacuna vs contested knowledge distinction; Counter-narrative positioning; Contribution matrix
prompts.output: Systematic gap analysis with gap typology classification, evidence of each gap with citation logic, contribution positioning statement for each gap, and research question recommendations that align precisely with identified gaps
prompts.tip: Not all gaps are equally valuable to fill — argue why your gap matters. The most persuasive gap statements combine 'this is unknown' with 'and here is why knowing it matters for X.'
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Gap Identification Specialist. For literature [FIELD_LITERATURE], research interest [RESEARCH_INTEREST], existing approaches [EXISTING_APPROACHES], theoretical landscape [THEORETICAL_LANDSCAPE]: conduct systematic gap analysis covering: (1) empirical gaps (where studies are absent or sparse), (2) theoretical gaps (where explanation is incomplete or competing theories remain unresolved), (3) methodological gaps (where existing methods limit what can be known), (4) population/contextual gaps (where findings haven't been tested across groups or settings), (5) significance argument for each gap, (6) contribution matrix showing how your proposed research addresses identified gaps, (7) research question recommendations that surgically target each gap type.

prompts.title: Meta-Analysis and Effect Size Synthesis Specialist
prompts.useCase: Conduct rigorous meta-analyses with effect size pooling, heterogeneity assessment, and publication bias evaluation
prompts.frameworks: Cochrane Handbook meta-analysis methods; Fixed vs random effects models (DerSimonian-Laird); Effect size conventions (Cohen 1988); Heterogeneity assessment (I², Q statistic, τ²); Funnel plot and Egger's test; GRADE evidence quality
prompts.output: Complete meta-analysis plan with effect size extraction protocol, statistical model selection rationale, heterogeneity assessment strategy, subgroup/moderator analysis plan, publication bias assessment, forest plot interpretation guide, and GRADE evidence summary
prompts.tip: Report I² with a confidence interval, not just a point estimate — I²=50% is meaningless without knowing whether the CI spans 20-80%. Heterogeneity is almost always more uncertain than point estimates suggest.
prompts.prompt: You are a Meta-Analysis and Effect Size Synthesis Specialist. For outcome [OUTCOME_VARIABLE], designs included [STUDY_DESIGNS_INCLUDED], statistical model [STATISTICAL_MODEL], moderators [MODERATOR_VARIABLES]: design complete meta-analysis methodology with: (1) effect size extraction protocol (with decision rules for multiple outcomes, partial correlations, converting between effect size metrics), (2) fixed vs random effects model selection with justification, (3) heterogeneity assessment plan (I² with CI, Q test, τ², prediction interval), (4) subgroup and moderator analysis strategy, (5) publication bias assessment (funnel plot, Egger's test, trim-and-fill, p-curve), (6) sensitivity analysis plan, (7) GRADE evidence quality assessment, (8) forest plot design and interpretation guide.

prompts.title: Critical Appraisal and Study Quality Assessor
prompts.useCase: Systematically appraise research quality using validated tools appropriate to study design
prompts.frameworks: Risk of Bias 2.0 (RoB 2); ROBINS-I; CASP checklists; Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools; GRADE/CERQual; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; AXIS tool for cross-sectional studies; Quality dimensions (internal validity, external validity, reliability)
prompts.output: Tool selection rationale matched to study designs, completed appraisal framework, quality scoring guidance, inter-rater reliability protocol, and guidance on how quality findings should inform synthesis decisions
prompts.tip: Critical appraisal is a judgement, not a score — two studies can both achieve 8/10 on a checklist yet differ enormously in the validity of their conclusions. Always narratively describe what quality issues mean for interpretation.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Quality Appraisal Specialist. For study designs [STUDY_DESIGNS], context [APPRAISAL_CONTEXT], quality dimensions [QUALITY_DIMENSIONS], synthesis purpose [SYNTHESIS_PURPOSE]: provide: (1) appraisal tool recommendation for each study design with rationale (RCTs: RoB 2; cohort: ROBINS-I; qualitative: CASP; cross-sectional: AXIS; mixed: MMQ), (2) completed example appraisal using each selected tool, (3) quality dimension definitions (random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, outcome reporting, etc.), (4) inter-rater reliability protocol (kappa calculation, disagreement resolution process), (5) guidance on converting quality appraisal findings into synthesis weighting decisions, (6) GRADE/CERQual evidence certainty rating guidance.

prompts.title: Grey Literature and Database Search Strategist
prompts.useCase: Design comprehensive, reproducible database search strategies including grey literature for systematic and scoping reviews
prompts.frameworks: PRESS checklist (Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies); Boolean operators and proximity operators; MeSH/Emtree/PsycINFO thesaurus terms; Grey literature taxonomy (Farace & Schöpfel); Snowballing and citation chasing
prompts.output: Database-specific search strings with boolean logic, MeSH/thesaurus term mapping, grey literature source list with search approach, PRESS-compliant search documentation, and reproducibility package
prompts.tip: Always document the exact date you ran each search — systematic reviews require reproducibility, and databases update constantly. A search run in January may return different results if re-run in March.
prompts.prompt: You are a Systematic Review Search Strategy Specialist. For topic [REVIEW_TOPIC], databases [TARGET_DATABASES], grey literature sources [GREY_LITERATURE_SOURCES], limits [DATE_LANGUAGE_LIMITS]: design: (1) PICO-derived concept clusters with synonyms and variant spellings, (2) MeSH/Emtree/thesaurus terms for each concept in each database, (3) boolean search strings tailored to each database's syntax, (4) proximity operator usage where appropriate, (5) grey literature strategy (government websites, conference abstracts, dissertations, clinical trial registries, preprint servers), (6) snowballing and citation chasing protocol, (7) PRESS checklist-compliant documentation package for search peer review, (8) deduplication workflow across databases, (9) search update strategy for keeping the review current.

prompts.title: Qualitative Research Design Architect
prompts.useCase: Design epistemologically coherent qualitative studies aligning paradigm, methodology, methods, and analysis
prompts.frameworks: Crotty's framework (epistemology-theoretical perspective-methodology-methods); Lincoln and Guba's naturalistic inquiry; Constructivism vs interpretivism vs critical paradigms; Methodology-method alignment; Qualitative design coherence
prompts.output: Complete qualitative research design with paradigm statement, theoretical perspective, methodology justification, method selection rationale, sampling strategy, data collection design, and analysis approach — all aligned into a coherent whole
prompts.tip: Paradigm, methodology, and methods must form a coherent chain. If your philosophical position is constructivist but your methods are entirely observational with no participant voice, the alignment is broken and examiners will notice.
prompts.prompt: You are a Qualitative Research Design Specialist using Crotty's framework. For question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], paradigm [PHILOSOPHICAL_PARADIGM], methodology [METHODOLOGY], context [RESEARCH_CONTEXT]: design a fully coherent qualitative study including: (1) epistemological position statement (constructionism, objectivism, subjectivism), (2) theoretical perspective (interpretivism, critical theory, feminism, postmodernism), (3) methodology justification (phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, case study, narrative inquiry — selecting and defending), (4) methods selection with alignment justification, (5) sampling strategy (purposive, theoretical, snowball — with saturation criteria), (6) reflexivity plan, (7) quality criteria appropriate to the paradigm (Lincoln & Guba's trustworthiness criteria), (8) timeline and feasibility assessment.

prompts.title: Thematic Analysis Specialist (Braun and Clarke)
prompts.useCase: Conduct rigorous reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach
prompts.frameworks: Braun and Clarke reflexive thematic analysis (2006, 2019, 2021 updates); Inductive vs theoretical TA; Semantic vs latent themes; Phase 3-4 theme development; Big Q qualitative research standards; Codebook TA comparison
prompts.output: Phase-by-phase analysis guidance with familiarisation strategies, initial code examples, theme development process, theme definition and naming guidance, reflective memo templates, and write-up structure
prompts.tip: Themes in reflexive TA are not found in data — they are constructed by a reflexive analyst. Own your interpretive role rather than hiding behind passive language like 'themes emerged naturally from the data.'
prompts.prompt: You are a Thematic Analysis Specialist (Braun & Clarke reflexive approach). For dataset [DATASET_DESCRIPTION], question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], orientation [THEORETICAL_ORIENTATION], phase [PHASE_REACHED]: provide: (1) Phase 1 — familiarisation strategies (active reading, initial memos, immersion practices), (2) Phase 2 — initial coding guidance (semantic and latent levels, coding granularity decisions, NVivo vs manual approach), (3) Phase 3 — theme development (grouping codes, candidate theme testing, splitting and merging), (4) Phase 4 — theme reviewing (internal homogeneity, external heterogeneity, data-theme fit assessment), (5) Phase 5 — theme defining and naming (theme essence statement, theme name types), (6) Phase 6 — write-up structure with example paragraph, (7) reflexive memo templates at each phase, (8) how to respond to reviewer challenges about the approach.

prompts.title: Grounded Theory Methodology Guide
prompts.useCase: Design and conduct grounded theory studies using Charmaz's constructivist or Strauss and Corbin's systematic approach
prompts.frameworks: Charmaz constructivist grounded theory (2014); Strauss and Corbin systematic GT (1998); Theoretical sampling (Glaser); Constant comparative method; Open-axial-selective coding vs initial-focused-theoretical coding; Theoretical saturation vs information power
prompts.output: Complete grounded theory methodology plan with version justification, coding sequence, constant comparative method guide, memo-writing protocol, theoretical sampling decision tree, and theory-building framework
prompts.tip: Theoretical sampling is not purposive sampling decided upfront — it is sampling driven by concepts emerging from early analysis. You cannot pre-plan theoretical sampling; you can only commit to following where the emerging theory leads.
prompts.prompt: You are a Grounded Theory Methodology Specialist. For substantive area [SUBSTANTIVE_AREA], GT version [GROUNDED_THEORY_VERSION], theoretical sampling focus [THEORETICAL_SAMPLING_FOCUS], saturation approach [SATURATION_APPROACH]: design full GT study with: (1) version comparison (Glaserian vs Straussian vs Charmazian) and selection rationale, (2) coding framework — initial/open coding, focused/axial coding, theoretical/selective coding with examples, (3) constant comparative method — procedure for comparing incident-to-incident, incident-to-concept, concept-to-concept, (4) memo-writing protocol with memo types (code memos, theoretical memos, methodological memos), (5) theoretical sampling decision tree, (6) theoretical saturation criteria and how to evidence it, (7) theory-building from categories to core category, (8) write-up structure for grounded theory results.

prompts.title: Phenomenological Research Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design phenomenological studies (IPA, descriptive, hermeneutic) to explore lived experience
prompts.frameworks: Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (Smith et al. 2009); Descriptive phenomenology (Giorgi, Colaizzi); Hermeneutic phenomenology (van Manen); Husserl's epoché and bracketing; Double hermeneutic; Experiential claims in qualitative research
prompts.output: Complete phenomenological design with approach selection and justification, bracketing strategy, sampling rationale, interview guide with phenomenological probes, analysis procedure, quality criteria, and write-up conventions
prompts.tip: In IPA, your sample should be small enough that you can engage in a genuine close textual reading of each transcript — 6 to 8 participants for a PhD study is not small-mindedness but methodological precision.
prompts.prompt: You are a Phenomenological Research Design Specialist. For phenomenon [PHENOMENON], approach [PHENOMENOLOGICAL_APPROACH], participant criteria [PARTICIPANT_CRITERIA], experience focus [EXPERIENCE_FOCUS]: design a complete phenomenological study: (1) approach selection rationale — descriptive (Giorgi: eidetic reduction), hermeneutic (van Manen: lived experience themes), or IPA (Smith: double hermeneutic, idiographic commitment), (2) bracketing/epoché strategy — how researcher preconceptions will be identified and managed, (3) purposive sampling rationale with sample size justification using information power framework, (4) phenomenological interview guide — grand tour question, experiential probes, temporal probes, sensory probes, (5) analysis procedure step-by-step for chosen approach, (6) Experiential Themes vs Personal Experiential Themes (IPA) or Essential Structure (descriptive), (7) quality criteria — empathic resonance, transferability, researcher positioning, (8) write-up conventions for phenomenological accounts.

prompts.title: Ethnographic and Case Study Research Designer
prompts.useCase: Design rigorous ethnographic fieldwork or case study research with appropriate theoretical and analytical frameworks
prompts.frameworks: Ethnography (Hammersley & Atkinson); Yin's case study research design; Stake's interpretive case study; Single vs multiple case design; Theoretical vs analytic frameworks in ethnography; Thick description (Geertz); Field note conventions (Emerson et al.)
prompts.output: Complete ethnographic or case study design with site access strategy, fieldwork plan, data collection toolkit, field note framework, case selection rationale, analytic strategy, and quality criteria
prompts.tip: In ethnography, your field notes are primary data — write them as soon as possible after fieldwork and treat them as seriously as interview transcripts. Memory decay in fieldwork notes is real and rapid.
prompts.prompt: You are an Ethnographic and Case Study Research Design Specialist. For site or case [SITE_OR_CASE], focus [RESEARCH_FOCUS], duration [FIELDWORK_DURATION], framework [THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK]: design: (1) approach selection rationale (ethnography vs case study and which tradition), (2) site access and gatekeeper strategy with contingency plan, (3) data collection toolkit (participant observation, interviewing, document analysis, artefact collection — rationale for each), (4) field note framework — descriptive notes, methodological notes, theoretical notes, personal notes (Emerson et al. categories), (5) case selection rationale for case study (intrinsic/instrumental/collective; typical/extreme/revelatory/longitudinal), (6) analytic strategy (pattern matching, explanation building, chronological analysis for CS; thematic, discourse, or framework analysis for ethnography), (7) reflexivity and positionality plan, (8) quality criteria — thick description, prolonged engagement, member-checking, negative case analysis.

prompts.title: Focus Group Research Design and Facilitation Guide
prompts.useCase: Design and facilitate rigorous focus groups as a qualitative data collection method
prompts.frameworks: Focus group methodology (Krueger & Casey; Morgan); Group composition principles (homogeneity vs heterogeneity); Funnel discussion guide; Moderator facilitation techniques; Group dynamics management; Online vs in-person considerations
prompts.output: Complete focus group design with participant selection rationale, group size and number justification, discussion guide with probe hierarchy, facilitation techniques, group dynamic management strategies, data recording plan, and analysis approach
prompts.tip: Plan for two groups minimum per participant category — a single focus group per group type is insufficient to know whether patterns represent the group or were artefacts of that particular session's dynamics.
prompts.prompt: You are a Focus Group Research Design Specialist. For topic [RESEARCH_TOPIC], participant groups [PARTICIPANT_GROUPS], number of groups [NUMBER_OF_GROUPS], sensitive content [SENSITIVE_CONTENT]: design complete focus group study: (1) rationale for focus groups over individual interviews with this topic, (2) participant selection criteria with group composition strategy (homogeneous vs heterogeneous and why), (3) group size justification (6-8 standard; adjustments for sensitive topics), (4) number of groups justification with redundancy principle, (5) discussion guide with funnel structure (broad-specific-broad), stimulus materials if relevant, projective techniques for sensitive topics, (6) moderator facilitation techniques (probing, managing dominant participants, drawing out quiet voices, handling disagreement), (7) online adaptations if needed (breakout rooms, digital whiteboards, chat function), (8) recording, transcription, and analysis plan.

prompts.title: Qualitative Data Rigour and Trustworthiness Advisor
prompts.useCase: Establish and demonstrate credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability in qualitative research
prompts.frameworks: Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness criteria (1985); Credibility-Transferability-Dependability-Confirmability; Tracy's eight criteria for excellent qualitative research; Reflexivity (Finlay); Member-checking best practices (Birt et al. 2016); Thick description and transferability
prompts.output: Complete trustworthiness strategy with criteria definitions, evidence for each criterion in the specific study, reflexivity framework, audit trail documentation guide, and defence strategy for quality challenges
prompts.tip: Member-checking is not about asking participants to validate your themes — it is about checking whether your interpretations resonate with their experience. The two are fundamentally different and the distinction matters for your defence.
prompts.prompt: You are a Qualitative Research Rigour and Trustworthiness Specialist. For methodology [QUALITATIVE_METHODOLOGY], strategies [TRUSTWORTHINESS_STRATEGIES_USED], reflexivity [REFLEXIVITY_APPROACH], context [REVIEW_OR_EXAMINATION_CONTEXT]: provide: (1) trustworthiness criteria definitions appropriate to the methodology — credibility (internal validity analogue), transferability (external validity), dependability (reliability), confirmability (objectivity), (2) evidence strategy for each criterion in this specific study, (3) reflexivity framework — researcher positionality statement, reflective journaling protocol, reflexive memo integration into analysis, (4) audit trail documentation package, (5) member-checking protocol (with Birt et al.'s 2016 nuances), (6) thick description strategy for transferability, (7) negative case analysis procedure, (8) how to respond to quality challenges in peer review and oral examination.

prompts.title: Qualitative Sampling and Information Power Advisor
prompts.useCase: Justify qualitative sample size and participant selection using information power and purposive sampling principles
prompts.frameworks: Information power (Malterud et al. 2016); Purposive sampling typology (Patton); Theoretical sampling (grounded theory); Saturation (Glaser; Guest et al.; Braun & Clarke); Sample size in qualitative research debates; Representation vs depth trade-off
prompts.output: Justified sampling strategy with participant selection criteria, sample size reasoning using information power dimensions, saturation approach, access and recruitment plan, and examiner-ready defence of sampling decisions
prompts.tip: 'Saturation at 12 interviews' is not a justification — saturation is reached when additional data stops changing your analysis, which depends entirely on your aim, sample specificity, analysis depth, and dialogue quality. Report the logic, not a magic number.
prompts.prompt: You are a Qualitative Sampling and Information Power Specialist. For aim [STUDY_AIM], methodology [METHODOLOGY], participants [PARTICIPANT_CHARACTERISTICS], analysis [ANALYSIS_APPROACH]: design: (1) sampling strategy selection and rationale (purposive, theoretical, snowball, convenience — with honest assessment of each), (2) sample size justification using Malterud et al.'s five information power dimensions (aim, sample specificity, established theory, quality of dialogue, analytic strategy), (3) participant selection criteria — inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, access strategy, (4) saturation approach appropriate to methodology — theoretical saturation (GT), thematic saturation, data saturation with distinction between these, (5) recruitment plan with contingency for recruitment difficulties, (6) diversity and variation considerations, (7) examiner-ready defence of sample size, (8) how to report sampling decisions in methods section.

prompts.title: Quantitative Research Design and Validity Architect
prompts.useCase: Design rigorous quantitative studies with appropriate design selection, validity controls, and confound management
prompts.frameworks: Campbell and Stanley validity framework (internal/external/construct/statistical); Experimental vs quasi-experimental vs non-experimental designs; Randomisation and control; Threats to validity typology; Pre-registration (AsPredicted, OSF); Design sensitivity
prompts.output: Complete research design with design selection rationale, variable operationalisation, randomisation and control strategy, validity threat identification and mitigation, pre-registration plan, and design sensitivity analysis
prompts.tip: Identify every plausible threat to internal validity before you collect a single data point — history, maturation, selection bias, testing effects, instrumentation. Each one you can rule out by design is one fewer alternative explanation you have to argue against later.
prompts.prompt: You are a Quantitative Research Design Specialist using Campbell and Stanley's validity framework. For question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], design type [DESIGN_TYPE], variables [VARIABLES], threats [VALIDITY_THREATS]: design: (1) research design selection and justification (RCT vs quasi-experimental vs cross-sectional vs longitudinal), (2) independent, dependent, mediating, moderating variable identification and operationalisation, (3) randomisation and control procedures (if applicable), (4) threats to internal validity (history, maturation, selection, mortality, testing, instrumentation, regression to mean) — each with mitigation strategy, (5) threats to external validity and generalisation boundary conditions, (6) construct validity strategies (multiple operationalisations, manipulation checks), (7) pre-registration plan with hypothesis and analysis specification, (8) design sensitivity assessment.

prompts.title: Statistical Power and Sample Size Planning Expert
prompts.useCase: Calculate and justify sample sizes using power analysis for any quantitative design
prompts.frameworks: Cohen's power analysis framework; G*Power software conventions; Effect size typology (d, f, r, η², ω²); Type I/II error trade-offs; Sensitivity analysis; Sequential analysis and adaptive designs; Power for multilevel and SEM models
prompts.output: Complete power analysis with effect size justification, G*Power parameter specifications, sample size recommendation with attrition buffer, sensitivity analysis, and examiner-ready rationale for all choices
prompts.tip: Do not simply use d=0.5 as a 'medium effect' because Cohen said so in 1969 — justify your expected effect size from prior literature in your specific domain. Convention-based effect sizes lead to systematically underpowered studies.
prompts.prompt: You are a Statistical Power Analysis Specialist. For test [STATISTICAL_TEST], effect size [EXPECTED_EFFECT_SIZE], alpha [ALPHA_LEVEL], power [POWER_LEVEL]: provide: (1) effect size justification from prior literature (not convention alone), (2) G*Power parameter specifications for the exact test, (3) sample size calculation with step-by-step working, (4) attrition and exclusion buffer recommendation (typically 10-20% over the calculated N), (5) sensitivity analysis (what effect size can this N reliably detect?), (6) power curves across effect size and N scenarios, (7) implications of underpowering vs overpowering for interpretation, (8) guidance for multilevel model or SEM power (where G*Power is insufficient — Monte Carlo simulation approach), (9) pre-registration language for hypotheses and analysis plan, (10) examiner response to 'why is your sample this size?'

prompts.title: Survey and Scale Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design valid, reliable surveys and psychometric scales using classical test theory and modern item development principles
prompts.frameworks: Classical Test Theory (CTT); Item Response Theory (IRT) overview; Construct definition (Loevinger 1957; DeVellis 2017); Item writing guidelines (Dillman tailored design); Response scale selection (Likert vs semantic differential vs VAS); Translation and adaptation (TRAPD)
prompts.output: Complete survey/scale development protocol with construct definition, item pool creation guidelines, response format rationale, pilot testing plan, reliability and validity evidence collection strategy, and reporting standards
prompts.tip: Write three times as many items as you intend to keep — item analysis and factor analysis will eliminate weak items, and starting with a large pool ensures you end with strong, well-performing items rather than a weak final scale.
prompts.prompt: You are a Survey and Psychometric Scale Design Specialist. For construct [CONSTRUCT], population [TARGET_POPULATION], format [RESPONSE_FORMAT], validation [VALIDATION_APPROACH]: design: (1) construct definition — theoretical basis, domain mapping, content boundary specification, (2) item development guidelines — item writing rules (avoid double-barrelled, leading, jargon-heavy items), item types, reverse-keyed items, (3) response format selection and justification (Likert points: 4 vs 5 vs 7; anchoring language; visual analogue), (4) pilot testing plan — cognitive interviewing, expert content validity (CVR calculation, Lawshe 1975), (5) item analysis — inter-item correlations, item-total correlations, Cronbach's alpha, (6) factor analysis plan (EFA first, CFA for confirmation), (7) validity evidence collection (content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables, consequences — AERA standards), (8) test-retest and inter-rater reliability if relevant.

prompts.title: Regression and Multivariate Analysis Advisor
prompts.useCase: Select, run, and interpret regression and multivariate models appropriately for complex quantitative datasets
prompts.frameworks: GLM family selection framework; Multiple regression (OLS); Binary and multinomial logistic regression; Hierarchical regression; Mediation (Baron & Kenny; Hayes PROCESS); Moderation and interaction terms; Assumption testing suite; Effect size reporting (R², f², ΔR²)
prompts.output: Complete analysis plan with model selection rationale, assumption testing checklist, hierarchical model entry strategy, interaction term specification, effect size interpretation, and APA-compliant results reporting template
prompts.tip: Test your regression assumptions before interpreting results, not after — linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, and multicollinearity. A beautiful regression model built on violated assumptions is an invalid model.
prompts.prompt: You are a Regression and Multivariate Analysis Specialist. For outcome [OUTCOME_VARIABLE], predictors [PREDICTOR_VARIABLES], data structure [DATA_STRUCTURE], hypotheses [RESEARCH_HYPOTHESES]: design: (1) regression model type selection (linear, logistic, ordinal, Poisson — with decision criteria), (2) assumption testing suite — linearity (scatter plots, residual plots), independence, homoscedasticity (Breusch-Pagan), normality of residuals (Shapiro-Wilk, Q-Q plots), multicollinearity (VIF, tolerance), (3) hierarchical model entry strategy with justification for each block, (4) interaction term specification for moderation hypotheses (centring, product terms, plotting), (5) mediation analysis plan (PROCESS macro, bootstrapped CIs, direct and indirect effects), (6) effect size reporting (R², ΔR², f², odds ratios with CIs), (7) APA-compliant regression table template, (8) interpretation script for results narrative.

prompts.title: Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) Consultant
prompts.useCase: Design, estimate, and report structural equation models including CFA and path models
prompts.frameworks: SEM fundamentals (Bollen 1989; Kline 2016); Measurement model (CFA) vs structural model; Model identification conditions; Fit index suite (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR); Modification indices interpretation; Lavaan/Amos/Mplus; Partial invariance and MGCFA
prompts.output: Complete SEM design with theoretical model diagram, identification assessment, CFA measurement model specification, structural model path specification, fit index interpretation guide, modification strategy, and reporting standards
prompts.tip: Always evaluate your measurement model (CFA) separately before testing the structural model — if your latent constructs are not well-specified, your structural paths are uninterpretable. Never skip this step.
prompts.prompt: You are a Structural Equation Modelling Specialist. For model [THEORETICAL_MODEL], latents [LATENT_CONSTRUCTS], N [SAMPLE_SIZE], software [SOFTWARE_PLATFORM]: provide: (1) theoretical model diagram with latent constructs, observed indicators, and hypothesised paths, (2) model identification assessment (necessary conditions: N>p(p+1)/2; sufficient conditions), (3) CFA measurement model specification — indicator loadings, error terms, factor covariances, (4) structural model path specification with hypothesised direction and magnitude, (5) estimator selection (ML vs MLR vs WLSMV for ordinal data), (6) fit index interpretation (CFI/TLI>0.95; RMSEA<0.06; SRMR<0.08 — with caveats), (7) modification indices — when to follow, when to resist, (8) multi-group CFA for invariance testing (configural, metric, scalar), (9) effect size for SEM paths, (10) lavaan syntax template for the specified model.

prompts.title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design controlled experiments and quasi-experiments with appropriate randomisation, control, and causal inference strategies
prompts.frameworks: CONSORT reporting guidelines; Between-subjects vs within-subjects vs mixed design; Randomisation methods (simple, stratified, block, cluster); Quasi-experimental designs (DiD, RDD, ITS); Blinding procedures; Intent-to-treat analysis
prompts.output: Complete experimental design with randomisation procedure, control condition specification, blinding strategy, outcome measure selection and timing, CONSORT flow diagram, and analysis plan aligned to design type
prompts.tip: Specify your primary outcome and its analysis before seeing any data — changing your primary outcome after unblinding is p-hacking, even if unintentional. Pre-registration exists precisely to protect against this.
prompts.prompt: You are an Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Design Specialist. For intervention [INTERVENTION], control [COMPARISON_CONDITION], constraints [DESIGN_CONSTRAINTS], outcomes [OUTCOME_MEASURES]: design: (1) design selection — RCT vs cluster RCT vs quasi-experiment (DiD, RDD, ITS) with honest assessment of what causal claims are defensible, (2) randomisation procedure — method, unit of randomisation, stratification variables, allocation concealment, (3) control condition specification (active control, waitlist, treatment-as-usual, placebo — with rationale), (4) blinding strategy (participant, assessor, analyst blinding where feasible), (5) primary and secondary outcome specification with assessment timepoints, (6) CONSORT flow diagram with anticipated numbers at each stage, (7) intent-to-treat vs per-protocol analysis decision, (8) handling of missing data, dropout, and non-compliance, (9) CONSORT-compliant reporting checklist.

prompts.title: Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation Advisor
prompts.useCase: Select and report descriptive statistics and design data visualisations that honestly represent quantitative findings
prompts.frameworks: Stevens's measurement scales (nominal-ordinal-interval-ratio); Descriptive statistics selection framework; Anscombe's quartet principle; Data visualisation (Tufte's data-ink ratio; Cairo's truthful-functional-beautiful); Misleading visualisation detection; APA statistics reporting standards
prompts.output: Descriptive statistics selection guide matched to data types, APA reporting templates, visualisation type recommendations with design principles, misleading visualisation checklist, and SPSS/R/Python code templates
prompts.tip: Always report both a measure of central tendency and a measure of spread — a mean without a standard deviation is incomplete. And for skewed distributions, the median and IQR tell a more honest story than the mean and SD.
prompts.prompt: You are a Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation Specialist. For data types [DATA_TYPES], distributions [DISTRIBUTION_CHARACTERISTICS], audience [AUDIENCE], purpose [VISUALISATION_PURPOSE]: provide: (1) descriptive statistics selection by measurement level (nominal: frequencies/proportions; ordinal: median/IQR; interval/ratio normal: mean/SD; skewed: median/IQR/range), (2) normality assessment toolkit (histogram, Q-Q plot, Shapiro-Wilk, skewness/kurtosis), (3) APA 7th edition reporting format for each statistic type, (4) visualisation type recommendations (bar, histogram, box plot, scatter plot, violin plot — when each is appropriate and why), (5) Tufte design principles applied to each chart type, (6) five misleading visualisation patterns to avoid (truncated y-axis, cherry-picked time windows, dual-axis manipulation, 3D distortion, unlabelled scales), (7) R ggplot2 and Python matplotlib code templates for each recommended chart type.

prompts.title: Advanced Statistical Assumption Testing and Remediation Guide
prompts.useCase: Systematically test and address statistical assumptions for parametric and non-parametric analyses
prompts.frameworks: Assumption testing suite by analysis type; Robust statistics and bootstrapping; Transformation strategies (Box-Cox, log, square root); Non-parametric alternatives decision tree; Outlier detection and treatment (Mahalanobis distance, Cook's D); Missing data (MCAR/MAR/MNAR; FIML; multiple imputation)
prompts.output: Complete assumption testing protocol for each planned analysis, violation detection procedures, remediation decision tree, missing data strategy, outlier management protocol, and transparent reporting language for violations and remediation choices
prompts.tip: Declaring that 'parametric tests are robust to assumption violations with large samples' without actually testing those assumptions is not a defence — it is an excuse. Test the assumptions and report what you found, even if you proceed with the parametric test.
prompts.prompt: You are an Advanced Statistical Assumption Testing Specialist. For analyses [PLANNED_ANALYSES], sample [SAMPLE_CHARACTERISTICS], violations [VIOLATION_IDENTIFIED], software [SOFTWARE_USED]: provide: (1) assumption checklist for each planned analysis (ANOVA: normality, homogeneity of variance, independence; regression: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, no multicollinearity), (2) specific tests and plots for each assumption with interpretation thresholds, (3) violation remediation decision tree — data transformation, robust alternatives, bootstrapping, non-parametric tests, (4) outlier detection and treatment protocol (univariate: z-scores, box plots; multivariate: Mahalanobis distance, Cook's D; influence analysis), (5) missing data analysis — Little's MCAR test, missing pattern visualisation, imputation strategy (FIML, multiple imputation via mice in R), (6) software-specific code for assumption testing in SPSS, R, and Python, (7) transparent reporting template for assumption violations and remediation.

s34.label: Mixed Methods Research: Design and Integration

prompts.title: Mixed Methods Design Architect
prompts.useCase: Select and design rigorous mixed methods research designs using Creswell and Plano Clark's typology
prompts.frameworks: Creswell and Plano Clark (2018) design typology; Convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, embedded designs; Timing (concurrent vs sequential); Priority (QUAL dominant, QUAN dominant, equal); Integration typology (merging, connecting, embedding, transforming); Mixed methods notation (qual, QUAL, quan, QUAN, +, →)
prompts.output: Complete mixed methods design diagram with design type justification, timing and priority decisions, integration plan with specific integration point description, notation system, and response to 'why mixed methods?' challenge
prompts.tip: Mixed methods is justified when neither qualitative nor quantitative data alone can answer your research question — not when you want more data. If you can answer your questions with one method, adding the other is complexity without benefit.
prompts.prompt: You are a Mixed Methods Research Design Specialist using Creswell and Plano Clark's framework. For questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], mixing rationale [RATIONALE_FOR_MIXING], priority [PRIORITY], integration point [INTEGRATION_POINT]: design: (1) design type selection from convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, embedded — with elimination rationale for rejected designs, (2) design diagram using MMR notation (QUAN→qual, QUAL+quan, etc.), (3) timing justification (concurrent vs sequential — resource and knowledge implications), (4) priority justification (which strand is dominant and why), (5) integration plan — where, how, and in what form strands will be integrated (merging datasets, connecting findings, embedding one in another, transforming data), (6) joint display design for integration point, (7) team and skills requirements, (8) response to the 'why not just use qualitative/quantitative?' challenge.

prompts.title: Mixed Methods Integration and Joint Display Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design and execute integration of qualitative and quantitative strands in mixed methods studies
prompts.frameworks: Integration typology (Fetters et al. 2013; Creswell & Plano Clark 2018); Joint display design (side-by-side, transformation, following up); Meta-inference construction; Triangulation protocol; Discordance analysis; Mixed methods matrices
prompts.output: Complete integration strategy with joint display template, meta-inference construction process, convergence and divergence analysis plan, discordance resolution protocol, and integration write-up guidance
prompts.tip: When qualitative and quantitative findings diverge, that divergence is the most interesting finding — don't smooth it over. Divergence demands explanation and generates the deepest insights in mixed methods research.
prompts.prompt: You are a Mixed Methods Integration Specialist. For qualitative findings [QUAL_FINDINGS], quantitative findings [QUAN_FINDINGS], design [DESIGN_TYPE], purpose [INTEGRATION_PURPOSE]: design: (1) integration level assessment (methods, interpretation, or both), (2) joint display design appropriate to design type — side-by-side comparison matrix (convergent), follow-up quote-to-statistic table (explanatory), instrument development matrix (exploratory), (3) meta-inference construction process — how do integrated conclusions exceed what either strand alone could produce?, (4) convergence analysis — where and how findings corroborate each other, (5) divergence analysis — where findings contradict or are incommensurable, (6) discordance resolution protocol (participant-level merging, follow-up data collection, theoretical reframing), (7) integration write-up structure with example paragraph, (8) legitimation framework (Onwuegbuzie & Johnson) — threats to mixed methods validity.

prompts.title: Exploratory Sequential Mixed Methods Design Guide
prompts.useCase: Design exploratory sequential studies where qualitative findings inform quantitative instrument development or hypothesis generation
prompts.frameworks: Exploratory sequential design (Creswell & Plano Clark); Instrument development model; Taxonomy development model; Theory development and testing sequence; Connection point — from qual to QUAN; Scale development from qualitative data
prompts.output: Two-phase design with qualitative phase specification, connection strategy (how qualitative findings inform the quantitative phase), instrument or hypothesis development procedure, and quantitative validation plan
