prompts.tip: The connection point in exploratory sequential design — where qualitative findings are transformed into quantitative instruments or hypotheses — is the most technically demanding step and the one most often underdescribed. Plan it in as much detail as either strand.
prompts.prompt: You are an Exploratory Sequential Mixed Methods Design Specialist. For phenomenon [UNEXPLORED_PHENOMENON], qualitative phase [QUALITATIVE_PHASE_DESIGN], instrument goal [INSTRUMENT_DEVELOPMENT_GOAL], validation plan [QUANTITATIVE_VALIDATION_PLAN]: design: (1) Phase 1 qualitative design — methodology, sampling, data collection, analysis (tailored to generate findings usable for Phase 2 development), (2) connection procedure — how qualitative findings will be transformed into QUAN strand inputs: themes → items (instrument development model) or themes → variables/hypotheses (theory development model) or typologies → frameworks (taxonomy model), (3) item generation from qualitative codes and themes (with examples), (4) content validity procedures before quantitative phase, (5) Phase 2 quantitative design — design, sampling (different from Phase 1), measures, analysis, (6) how Phase 2 validates, extends, or tests Phase 1 findings, (7) integration write-up — how to narrate the two-phase connection.

prompts.title: Explanatory Sequential Mixed Methods Design Guide
prompts.useCase: Design explanatory sequential studies where quantitative findings are explained and elaborated by qualitative follow-up
prompts.frameworks: Explanatory sequential design; Follow-up explanations model; Participant selection model; Connection point — from QUAN to qual; Purposive sampling from quantitative results; Building on significant results; Explaining outliers and surprising findings
prompts.output: Two-phase design with quantitative phase specification, connection strategy, purposive sampling from quantitative results, qualitative phase design to explain specific findings, and integration narrative
prompts.tip: In explanatory sequential design, the most powerful qualitative participants are often those at the extremes of your quantitative distributions — the highest scorers, lowest scorers, and outliers — not a random sample of your quantitative participants.
prompts.prompt: You are an Explanatory Sequential Mixed Methods Design Specialist. For quantitative findings [QUANTITATIVE_FINDINGS], follow-up questions [FOLLOW_UP_QUESTIONS], participant selection [QUALITATIVE_PARTICIPANT_SELECTION], explanation focus [EXPLANATION_FOCUS]: design: (1) Phase 1 quantitative design — design, measures, analysis, and specifically what findings will trigger Phase 2, (2) connection decision rules — which specific findings need qualitative explanation (significant results, outliers, group differences, unexpected patterns), (3) purposive participant selection from Phase 1 sample — how quantitative scores/profiles will guide qualitative sampling (extreme case, typical case, stratified purpose sampling from QUAN results), (4) Phase 2 qualitative design calibrated to explain specific QUAN findings — research questions reframed for explanation, interview guide targeting the QUAN results, (5) integration — how qualitative explanations will be layered onto quantitative findings in the final narrative, (6) example of how a specific quantitative finding would be explained qualitatively.

prompts.title: Mixed Methods Quality and Rigour Evaluator
prompts.useCase: Evaluate and strengthen rigour across both strands and at the integration point in mixed methods studies
prompts.frameworks: Mixed methods legitimation framework (Onwuegbuzie & Johnson 2006); Mixed methods quality criteria (O'Cathain 2010); Strand-specific rigour (Lincoln & Guba; Campbell & Stanley); Integration legitimation — inside-outside, fundamental difference, commensurability, conversion legitimation; MMAT appraisal tool
prompts.output: Strand-specific rigour assessment, integration-level quality evaluation, legitimation threat identification with mitigation, MMAT appraisal guidance, and write-up language for mixed methods quality
prompts.tip: Mixed methods studies must satisfy quality criteria at three levels: qualitative strand quality, quantitative strand quality, and integration quality — most researchers address the first two but neglect the third, which is precisely what makes a study mixed methods rather than two parallel mono-method studies.
prompts.prompt: You are a Mixed Methods Rigour and Quality Specialist. For design [MIXED_METHODS_DESIGN], qual strategies [QUAL_RIGOUR_STRATEGIES], quan strategies [QUAN_RIGOUR_STRATEGIES], integration [INTEGRATION_QUALITY]: provide: (1) qualitative strand rigour assessment using Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness criteria, (2) quantitative strand rigour assessment using validity and reliability framework, (3) integration-level quality using Onwuegbuzie and Johnson's legitimation framework: sample integration, inside-outside, weakness minimisation, sequential, conversion, paradigmatic mixing, commensurability, and multiple validities legitimation, (4) MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) self-assessment, (5) O'Cathain's quality indicators for MMR (good reporting, rigour in each strand, coherence between strands, added value from mixing), (6) examiner and reviewer challenge anticipation and response script, (7) quality write-up language for methods section.

prompts.title: Mixed Methods Research Question and Framework Designer
prompts.useCase: Develop integrated mixed methods research questions and conceptual frameworks that justify and guide the mixing rationale
prompts.frameworks: Mixed methods research question typology (Creswell; Plano Clark; Teddlie & Tashakkori); Central mixed methods question plus strand questions; MMR conceptual framework construction; Philosophical worldview for MMR (pragmatism; transformative; dialectical stance); Mixing rationale typology
prompts.output: Integrated research question set (central MMR question, QUAL questions, QUAN hypotheses), mixing rationale statement, conceptual framework diagram showing how strands relate, and philosophical worldview positioning
prompts.tip: Your mixed methods research question should articulate why you need both strands — it should be answerable only through integration, not through either strand alone. If you could answer it with qualitative data only, you haven't written a mixed methods question.
prompts.prompt: You are a Mixed Methods Research Question and Framework Design Specialist. For problem [RESEARCH_PROBLEM], qualitative focus [WHAT_QUAL_ADDRESSES], quantitative focus [WHAT_QUAN_ADDRESSES], framework [THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK]: design: (1) central mixed methods research question — which requires integration to answer, (2) QUAL strand questions — what qualitative inquiry will address (open, exploratory, experience-focused), (3) QUAN strand hypotheses or questions — what quantitative inquiry will address (specific, measurable, directional), (4) mixing rationale statement — triangulation/complementarity/expansion/initiation/development (Greene et al. 1989 typology) — which applies and why, (5) conceptual framework diagram showing: theoretical framework, QUAL strand, QUAN strand, integration point, and how findings from each strand relate to the overarching question, (6) philosophical worldview positioning (pragmatism, transformative, dialectical) with justification, (7) response to 'are your two strands really integrated?' challenge.

prompts.title: Research Ethics Application and IRB/Ethics Board Navigator
prompts.useCase: Design ethics applications for any research type — from minimal risk to complex vulnerable populations
prompts.frameworks: Belmont Report (respect for persons, beneficence, justice); TCPS2 (Canada); Declaration of Helsinki; Common Rule 45 CFR 46; Risk-benefit assessment framework; Vulnerable population protections (subpart B/C/D); Informed consent elements (21 CFR 50.25)
prompts.output: Complete ethics application components: risk-benefit analysis, informed consent form, participant recruitment materials, data protection plan, vulnerable population safeguards, and examiner-ready justification for each ethical decision
prompts.tip: IRB reviewers read thousands of applications — write your risk-benefit analysis as if the reviewer knows nothing about your field. Jargon-free, explicit, and specific always beats technically accurate but opaque.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Ethics Application Specialist. For study [STUDY_DESIGN], participants [PARTICIPANT_POPULATION], data sensitivity [DATA_SENSITIVITY], institution [INSTITUTION_TYPE]: draft a complete ethics application package including: (1) risk classification with justification (minimal, greater than minimal, full board), (2) risk-benefit analysis using Belmont Report principles — respect for persons (autonomy, consent), beneficence (maximising benefits, minimising harm), justice (fair selection, equitable burden-sharing), (3) informed consent form with all 21 CFR 50.25 required elements in plain language (8th grade reading level), (4) participant recruitment script and materials, (5) data security and confidentiality plan, (6) vulnerable population safeguards if applicable, (7) deception justification and debriefing protocol if applicable, (8) response strategy for common board concerns about this design.

prompts.title: Research Integrity and Misconduct Prevention Advisor

prompts.frameworks: QRP (Questionable Research Practices) taxonomy; HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known); p-hacking and outcome switching; COPE guidelines; Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) framework; Pre-registration as integrity tool; Data fabrication, falsification, plagiarism (FFP) definitions
prompts.output: Research integrity audit checklist for each project stage, QRP identification and prevention strategies, pre-registration guidance, authorship ethics framework, data management integrity protocol, and procedures for responding to integrity concerns
prompts.tip: Pre-registration is the single most powerful integrity tool available to quantitative researchers — it separates confirmatory from exploratory analysis, eliminates outcome-switching, and makes your null results publishable.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Integrity Specialist. For context [RESEARCH_CONTEXT], concern [INTEGRITY_CONCERN], team [TEAM_STRUCTURE], stage [PUBLICATION_STAGE]: provide: (1) QRP taxonomy relevant to this context — HARKing, p-hacking, selective reporting, undisclosed flexibility, optional stopping, outcome switching — with real examples and consequences, (2) study design integrity checklist (pre-registration, power analysis, analysis plan, stopping rules), (3) data collection integrity procedures (audit trail, blinding, inter-rater reliability), (4) analysis integrity practices (transparent code, reproducible pipeline, sensitivity analyses), (5) reporting integrity — CONSORT/STROBE/PRISMA compliance, all outcomes reported, (6) authorship ethics using ICMJE criteria — who qualifies, how to handle disputes, ghost authorship, (7) data sharing and open science obligations, (8) procedures for reporting suspected misconduct.

prompts.title: Informed Consent Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Write ethically rigorous, participant-centred informed consent documents for any research population
prompts.frameworks: FDA 21 CFR 50.25 required elements; Plain language standards (Flesch-Kincaid Grade 8 target); Teach-back method; Process consent for longitudinal studies; Assent for minors; Capacity assessment; Waiver of consent criteria
prompts.output: Complete consent document with all required elements, plain-language version, visual/simplified version outline, assent form for minors if needed, and capacity assessment guidance for vulnerable populations
prompts.tip: Consent is a process, not a form — the document is evidence that the conversation happened. Design consent procedures first (how will you actually ensure understanding?), then write the form to document that process.
prompts.prompt: You are an Informed Consent Design Specialist. For procedures [STUDY_PROCEDURES], literacy level [PARTICIPANT_LITERACY], risks and benefits [RISKS_AND_BENEFITS], special circumstances [SPECIAL_CIRCUMSTANCES]: write: (1) full informed consent document with all eight required elements (purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, voluntary participation, contact information), (2) plain-language version at Grade 8 reading level (Flesch-Kincaid verified), (3) teach-back question set to verify participant comprehension, (4) assent form for minors aged 7–17 if applicable — developmentally appropriate language, (5) capacity assessment protocol for cognitively vulnerable participants, (6) process consent procedures for longitudinal studies (re-consent triggers, amendment notifications), (7) e-consent adaptations for online research, (8) waiver of consent justification template if full consent is not feasible.

prompts.title: Research Data Privacy and GDPR/HIPAA Compliance Guide
prompts.useCase: Design data privacy strategies compliant with GDPR, HIPAA, and institutional data governance for research projects
prompts.frameworks: GDPR (Regulation 2016/679) — lawful basis, data minimisation, purpose limitation, storage limitation; HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification (45 CFR 164.514); Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA); Anonymisation vs pseudonymisation distinction; FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)
prompts.output: Data privacy compliance plan covering lawful basis, consent language, anonymisation procedures, data transfer agreements, retention schedule, breach response protocol, and DPIA if needed
prompts.tip: Pseudonymisation (replacing identifiers with codes) is not anonymisation (irreversibly removing all identifiers) — GDPR treats them differently. True anonymisation removes research data from GDPR scope entirely; pseudonymised data is still personal data.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Data Privacy and Compliance Specialist. For data [DATA_TYPES_COLLECTED], jurisdictions [JURISDICTIONS], sharing [DATA_SHARING_PLANS], retention [RETENTION_PERIOD]: design: (1) GDPR lawful basis identification for research data (Article 6 and 9 — public interest in research as Article 9(2)(j) basis), (2) data minimisation and purpose limitation compliance strategy, (3) anonymisation vs pseudonymisation decision for each data type with procedure specification, (4) HIPAA de-identification method (Safe Harbor vs Expert Determination) if US health data involved, (5) data transfer agreements for international collaboration (Standard Contractual Clauses post-Schrems II), (6) data retention schedule with deletion procedures, (7) Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) trigger assessment and full DPIA outline if required, (8) participant rights response procedures (access, rectification, erasure, portability), (9) data breach response protocol.

prompts.title: Ethical Research with Vulnerable and Marginalised Populations Advisor
prompts.useCase: Design ethically robust research protocols for vulnerable, marginalised, or hard-to-reach populations

prompts.output: Comprehensive ethical protocol for vulnerable population research including community engagement strategy, power imbalance mitigation, trauma-informed procedures, culturally appropriate consent, and community benefit design

prompts.prompt: You are an Ethical Research with Vulnerable Populations Specialist. For population [POPULATION_GROUP], topic [RESEARCH_TOPIC], power dynamics [POWER_DYNAMICS], context [COMMUNITY_CONTEXT]: design: (1) vulnerability assessment — intrinsic vulnerability (cognitive, developmental, illness-related) vs situational vulnerability (incarceration, economic coercion, dependency relationship) and implications for each, (2) community engagement strategy before research begins — CBPR principles, community advisory boards, co-design approach, (3) power imbalance identification and mitigation strategies, (4) trauma-informed research procedures — anticipating trauma responses, researcher wellbeing, referral pathways, safety protocols, (5) culturally appropriate consent and communication, (6) decolonising research practices (Tuhiwai Smith): centering community knowledge, avoiding extractive research, reciprocity, (7) Indigenous data sovereignty (CARE principles) if applicable, (8) benefit-sharing and community return of findings plan, (9) IRB justification for research with this population.

prompts.title: Publication Ethics and Authorship Dispute Navigator
prompts.useCase: Navigate authorship decisions, submission ethics, and publication integrity challenges
prompts.frameworks: ICMJE authorship criteria (four conditions); CRediT taxonomy (14 contributor roles); COPE flowcharts for authorship disputes; Duplicate publication, salami-slicing, and self-plagiarism definitions; Conflict of interest disclosure requirements; Retraction ethics
prompts.output: Authorship allocation recommendation using ICMJE and CRediT, contributor statement template, conflict of interest disclosure, submission ethics checklist, and resolution pathways for authorship disputes
prompts.tip: According to ICMJE, all four criteria must be met for authorship — conception/design OR data acquisition OR analysis; AND drafting OR revising critically; AND final approval; AND accountability. Data collection alone does not qualify someone as an author.
prompts.prompt: You are a Publication Ethics and Authorship Specialist. For situation [AUTHORSHIP_SITUATION], journal [JOURNAL_REQUIREMENTS], COI [CONFLICT_OF_INTEREST], previous publication [PREVIOUS_PUBLICATION_STATUS]: provide: (1) ICMJE four-criteria authorship assessment for each contributor — who qualifies as author, who should be acknowledged, (2) CRediT taxonomy allocation for each contributor (14 roles: conceptualisation, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation, resources, data curation, writing-original draft, writing-review & editing, visualisation, supervision, project administration, funding acquisition), (3) author order negotiation guidance (first, corresponding, last authorship conventions by discipline), (4) conflict of interest identification and disclosure template, (5) duplicate publication and self-plagiarism risk assessment (threshold: typically >10% text overlap requires prior permission or disclosure), (6) COPE flowchart navigation for authorship disputes, (7) resolution strategy for specific dispute scenario described, (8) retraction and correction decision framework if needed.

prompts.title: Research Data Management Plan (DMP) Designer

prompts.output: Complete DMP covering data collection and formats, organisation and documentation, storage and backup, security, sharing and access, preservation, and funder-specific compliance elements

prompts.title: Open Science and Reproducibility Framework Advisor

For type [RESEARCH_TYPE], goals [OPEN_SCIENCE_GOALS], constraints [CONSTRAINTS], stage [CAREER_STAGE]: design an open science implementation plan: (1) pre-registration strategy — platform selection (OSF vs AsPredicted vs PROSPERO), what to pre-register (hypotheses, design, analysis plan, exclusion criteria), how to handle deviations, (2) Registered Reports pathway — advantages for your field, journal finder, Stage 1 vs Stage 2 protocol, (3) open data preparation — de-identification procedures, codebook and README writing, licence selection, repository selection, timing of release, (4) open materials — supplementary methods, stimuli, instruments, codebooks, (5) open code — version control (Git), code documentation standards, computational environment specification (Docker, renv, conda), (6) preprint strategy — when to post, which server, bioRxiv vs PsyArXiv vs SSRN, managing preprint-to-publication transition, (7) open access — green vs gold, preprint policy, SHERPA/RoMEO compliance, (8) career navigation — how to communicate open science contributions in job applications.

prompts.title: Research Dataset Documentation and Metadata Specialist

prompts.title: Reproducible Research Pipeline and Code Documentation Guide

prompts.prompt: You are a Reproducible Research Pipeline Design Specialist. For software [ANALYSIS_SOFTWARE], complexity [PROJECT_COMPLEXITY], team [COLLABORATION_SIZE], archiving [ARCHIVING_REQUIREMENTS]: design: (1) project folder structure (data/raw, data/processed, code/analysis, code/figures, output, docs) with naming conventions, (2) Git workflow — repository setup, branching strategy (main, dev, feature branches), commit message conventions, tagging releases, (3) environment management — R: renv.lock file, DESCRIPTION; Python: requirements.txt, conda environment.yml, or Docker image; (4) literate programming — R Markdown or Quarto document structure for analysis narrative + code + output in one document, (5) workflow automation — Makefile or Snakemake workflow connecting data → analysis → output with dependency tracking, (6) code documentation standards — function documentation (roxygen2 for R, docstrings for Python), inline comments, analysis script headers, (7) code review checklist for collaborative projects, (8) archiving package for publication — what to deposit in Zenodo with the paper, DOI assignment, (9) README template for the code repository.

prompts.title: Secondary Data Analysis and Existing Dataset Research Designer
prompts.useCase: Design rigorous secondary analysis studies using existing datasets, administrative records, or published data

prompts.output: Complete secondary analysis design with dataset evaluation, research question calibration, measurement alignment analysis, limitation identification, access procedure, analysis plan, and reporting standards

prompts.prompt: You are a Secondary Data Analysis Design Specialist. For dataset [TARGET_DATASET], question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], limitations [DATA_LIMITATIONS], access [ACCESS_PROCEDURE]: design: (1) dataset evaluation — provenance, collection methodology, representativeness, known limitations, citation requirements, (2) research question calibration — aligning theoretical constructs with available measures, scope condition setting, (3) measurement alignment analysis — how closely dataset variables match intended constructs, known measurement error, (4) data access procedure — application process, data use agreements, secure access environments (ONS SRS, UKDS, ICPSR), (5) data preparation plan — variable selection, recoding, derived variable construction, missing data assessment, (6) analytical strategy appropriate to data structure (cross-sectional, longitudinal, hierarchical), (7) limitations reporting — temporal mismatch, measurement limitations, selection bias, non-response, (8) reporting standards for secondary analysis — RECORD checklist for administrative data, data citation standards.

prompts.title: AI-Assisted Research Tools and Research Integrity Advisor

For stage [RESEARCH_STAGE], tools [AI_TOOLS_USED], disclosure [DISCLOSURE_REQUIREMENTS], concerns [INTEGRITY_CONCERNS]: provide: (1) stage-by-stage appropriate AI use guide — literature searching (with hallucination warnings), writing assistance, coding (Copilot, Code Interpreter), data analysis, grant writing, peer review (prohibited at most journals), (2) AI limitations researchers must understand — citation hallucination (never trust unretrieved citations), training data cutoffs, confident-sounding errors, lack of disciplinary depth, (3) verification workflow — how to independently verify every AI output before including in research, (4) disclosure templates for: manuscript methods section, grant applications, institutional systems, (5) COPE and major journal AI policy summary for the target publication, (6) AI authorship boundary — why AI cannot be an author, how to attribute AI assistance ethically, (7) integrity boundaries — what constitutes academic misconduct with AI assistance in your institution's context, (8) practical workflow for using AI effectively while protecting research integrity.

prompts.title: Discourse and Critical Discourse Analysis Specialist
prompts.useCase: Apply discourse analysis (DA) and critical discourse analysis (CDA) to examine language, power, and ideology in texts
prompts.frameworks: Foucauldian discourse analysis; Fairclough's Critical Discourse Analysis (three-dimensional model); Laclau and Mouffe's discourse theory; van Dijk's Socio-cognitive CDA; Potter and Wetherell's discursive psychology; Gee's discourse analysis tools; APPRAISAL theory (Martin and White)

prompts.tip: CDA is explicitly political — it starts from the assumption that discourse reproduces or challenges power structures. If you use CDA, be transparent about your critical stance; claiming neutrality while using CDA is methodologically inconsistent.
prompts.prompt: You are a Discourse and Critical Discourse Analysis Specialist. For data [TEXT_OR_DATA_TYPE], tradition [ANALYTICAL_TRADITION], questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], framework [THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK]: design: (1) DA tradition selection and comparison (Foucauldian: subject positions, knowledge-power, discursive formations; Fairclough CDA: text, discourse practice, social practice; Discursive Psychology: rhetoric, variability, action orientation), (2) analytical framework specification with key concepts operationalised for this data, (3) text/corpus sampling strategy — representativeness, diversity, saturation in discourse terms, (4) multi-level analysis procedure (Fairclough): micro-linguistic (grammar, lexis, modality), meso-discursive (intertextuality, genre), macro-social (ideology, power relations), (5) analytical tools — transitivity, modality, presupposition, hedging, pronoun use, metaphor, nominalization analysis with worked text examples, (6) reflexivity and positionality in critical analysis, (7) write-up conventions for DA/CDA with example analytical paragraph.

prompts.title: Narrative Inquiry and Life History Research Designer
prompts.useCase: Design and conduct narrative inquiry studies that honour the storied nature of human experience
prompts.frameworks: Clandinin and Connelly's narrative inquiry (three-dimensional space); Polkinghorne's narrative analysis vs analysis of narratives; Riessman's narrative analysis typologies (thematic, structural, dialogic, visual); Labov and Waletzky's story grammar; Life history methodology; Storying and restorying
prompts.output: Complete narrative inquiry design with philosophical grounding, field text collection plan, narrative analysis approach, representation strategies, relational ethics framework, and write-up that honours participant voices
prompts.tip: In narrative inquiry, the relationship between researcher and participant IS the research — it is not a methodological side-issue. Clandinin and Connelly's relational ethics asks: how does your research serve this person's life, not just your academic career?
prompts.prompt: You are a Narrative Inquiry and Life History Research Specialist. For focus [NARRATIVE_FOCUS], grounding [THEORETICAL_GROUNDING], participants [PARTICIPANT_SELECTION], analysis [ANALYSIS_APPROACH]: design: (1) narrative inquiry philosophical grounding — experience as narrative (Dewey's experiential continuum, interaction, situation — Clandinin and Connelly's three-dimensional space), (2) field text collection methods — narrative interviews (McAdams life story protocol), documents, photographs, journals, field notes — and how each will be collected, (3) narrative analysis approach selection and justification: thematic (what is told), structural (how it is told), dialogic/performative (to whom and under what conditions), or visual narrative analysis, (4) Labov's story grammar if structural analysis — abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution, coda, (5) restorying process — moving from field texts to research texts, (6) representation strategies — narrative portraits, composite characters, poetic representation, (7) relational ethics — negotiating participant identities, member checks in narrative research (different from thematic analysis), giving back, (8) write-up that honours participant voice and researcher presence.

prompts.title: Action Research and Participatory Research Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design action research and participatory action research (PAR) studies that generate knowledge and drive real-world change
prompts.frameworks: Lewin's action research cycle (plan-act-observe-reflect); Kemmis and McTaggart's participatory action research; McNiff and Whitehead's living theory; Community-based participatory research (CBPR); Design-based research (DBR); Appreciative Inquiry (AI); Co-production principles
prompts.output: Complete action research design with problem framing, stakeholder engagement plan, cyclical methodology, data collection within cycles, reflection protocols, change documentation, and academic knowledge claim framework
prompts.tip: Action research generates two products simultaneously: practical change in the setting AND scholarly knowledge about that change. Both must be evident in your write-up — action without reflection is mere activity; reflection without action is armchair theorising.
prompts.prompt: You are an Action Research and Participatory Research Design Specialist. For context [PROBLEM_CONTEXT], stakeholders [STAKEHOLDER_GROUPS], goals [CHANGE_GOALS], cycles [CYCLES_PLANNED]: design: (1) problem framing — whose problem is this, how was it identified, what local knowledge already exists, (2) paradigm positioning — technical AR (efficiency focus), practical AR (professional development), emancipatory PAR (power and justice), (3) stakeholder engagement plan — who is included, in what roles (researchers, co-researchers, advisers), how power is shared, (4) cyclical methodology — Lewin's spiral adapted: problem identification → reconnaissance → planning → action → observation → reflection → re-planning, with specific activities and data at each stage, (5) data collection within cycles — what data, by whom, for what purpose at each cycle, (6) reflection protocols — structured reflective journals, group reflection meetings, critical friend roles, (7) change documentation and impact assessment, (8) academic knowledge claim framework — how to make defensible theoretical claims from action research, (9) write-up structure for AR that satisfies both practice and scholarly audiences.

prompts.title: Arts-Based and Creative Research Methods Advisor
prompts.useCase: Design studies using arts-based research methods — photovoice, digital storytelling, poetry, performance, visual methods
prompts.frameworks: Arts-Based Research (Barone and Eisner 2012); Photovoice (Wang and Burris 1997); Digital storytelling methodology; Poetic inquiry (Prendergast); A/r/tography; Performance ethnography; Visual research methods (Rose 2016); Research Creation
prompts.output: Complete arts-based research design with method rationale, participatory procedure, ethical considerations specific to creative methods, analysis approach for arts data, and dissemination strategy including public-facing and academic outputs
prompts.tip: Arts-based research must make an epistemological claim — that artistic processes reveal knowledge not accessible through conventional methods. If you cannot articulate what the art form makes knowable that words cannot, reconsider whether the method serves the question.
prompts.prompt: You are an Arts-Based Research Methods Specialist. For method [ARTS_METHOD], context [PARTICIPANT_CONTEXT], purpose [RESEARCH_PURPOSE], dissemination [DISSEMINATION_PLAN]: design: (1) arts method selection and epistemological justification — what does this method make visible that conventional methods cannot?, (2) specific method design: Photovoice: camera distribution, SHOWED discussion protocol, community exhibition; Digital storytelling: Center for DS 7-step process, story circle facilitation; Poetic inquiry: found poetry, interview poetry creation; Performance: devising process, verbatim theatre, (3) participatory facilitation plan — skill development for participants, creative process support, emotional safety, (4) ethical considerations specific to arts methods — ownership of artistic works, control over representation, emotional exposure, community exhibition consent, (5) analysis of arts data — aesthetic criticism (Barone and Eisner's criteria), thematic analysis of visual data (Rose's framework), poetic resonance assessment, (6) quality criteria for ABR — resonance, verisimilitude, transferability, catalytic validity, (7) dissemination strategy: academic (journal articles, conference), public (exhibition, performance, community return), (8) impact documentation.

prompts.title: Qualitative Longitudinal Research (QLR) Design Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design qualitative longitudinal studies that capture change, continuity, and process over time
prompts.frameworks: Qualitative longitudinal research methodology (Neale 2019; Thomson and Holland); Panel methodology vs follow-up vs time series; Wave design; Temporal analysis (synchronic vs diachronic); Repeat interviewing methodology; Attrition and missing cases in QLR; Temporal maps and timelines
prompts.output: Complete QLR design with time frame rationale, wave structure, repeat interview protocol, participant retention strategy, temporal analytical framework, cross-wave analysis approach, and presentation of longitudinal findings
prompts.tip: Qualitative longitudinal research is not just repeating qualitative data collection at intervals — it requires analytical frameworks specifically designed to understand time, change, and continuity. Plan your temporal analysis approach before the first wave, not after.
prompts.prompt: You are a Qualitative Longitudinal Research Design Specialist. For focus [LONGITUDINAL_FOCUS], timeframe [TIME_FRAME], retention [PARTICIPANT_RETENTION_STRATEGY], analysis [ANALYTICAL_APPROACH]: design: (1) QLR design rationale — why longitudinal, what processual or temporal questions drive it, what cross-sectional designs cannot answer, (2) wave structure — how many data collection points, spacing rationale, what changes at each wave, (3) repeat interview protocol — how to re-engage participants, memory and continuity in follow-up interviews, returning transcripts/summaries between waves, (4) participant retention strategy — maintaining engagement over time, handling dropout (distinguish by design from attrition), tracking procedures, (5) temporal analytical framework: synchronic analysis (within each wave), diachronic analysis (across waves, trajectories, turning points), (6) analytical tools for QLR — timeline construction, trajectory mapping, critical moment analysis, (7) handling attrition analytically — what absent cases tell you, missing data in QLR, (8) presenting longitudinal findings — narrative accounts, typologies of change, trajectory diagrams.

prompts.title: Qualitative Data Software (NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA) Workflow Guide
prompts.useCase: Design and implement QDAS-supported qualitative analysis workflows using NVivo, ATLAS.ti, or MAXQDA
prompts.frameworks: QDAS affordances and limitations; NVivo nodes vs ATLAS.ti codes vs MAXQDA code system; Teamwork functions in QDAS; Visualisation tools (models, maps, matrices); Reflexive TA in QDAS (Braun and Clarke's warnings); Audit trail functions; Mixed methods capabilities
prompts.output: Complete QDAS workflow design with software justification, project setup guide, coding workflow, team collaboration procedures, visual analysis strategy, and guidance on what QDAS can and cannot do for your methodology
prompts.tip: QDAS manages and organises qualitative data — it does not analyse it. The intellectual work of interpretation happens in your mind, not in the software. Researchers who treat code frequency counts as findings have confused management with analysis.
prompts.prompt: You are a Qualitative Data Analysis Software Specialist. For software [SOFTWARE_CHOICE], data [DATA_TYPES], methodology [ANALYSIS_METHODOLOGY], team [TEAM_COMPOSITION]: provide: (1) software comparison and selection rationale — NVivo (Mac/Windows, diverse data types, strong visualisation), ATLAS.ti (large projects, network views), MAXQDA (mixed methods integration, statistical links), free alternatives (QualCoder, Taguette), (2) project setup guide — folder structure, document import, source classification, memo system design, (3) coding workflow appropriate to methodology — reflective TA: use of memos over codes, grounded theory: memo-code integration, framework analysis: matrix approach, (4) team collaboration setup — role assignment, merge and reconcile procedures, inter-rater reliability in QDAS, (5) advanced features walkthrough — queries (text search, coding queries, matrix coding), visualisations (code co-occurrence maps, models, concept maps), (6) QDAS limitations by methodology — Braun and Clarke's critique of QDAS for reflexive TA, grounded theory's relationship with software, (7) audit trail documentation within QDAS, (8) export and reporting from QDAS to manuscript.

prompts.title: Reflexivity and Researcher Positionality Framework Builder
prompts.useCase: Develop a rigorous, theoretically grounded reflexivity framework for qualitative and interpretive research
prompts.frameworks: Reflexivity typology (personal, functional, disciplinary, political — Finlay 2002); Positionality statement construction; Insider/outsider continuum (Naples); Subjectivity-as-resource vs subjectivity-as-bias debate; Reflexive memo-writing (Clarke); Bracketing and epoché; Audit trail as reflexivity evidence
prompts.output: Comprehensive reflexivity framework with positionality statement, reflexive memo templates, analytical decision logging system, write-up sections for methods and discussion, and defence strategy for reflexivity challenges
prompts.tip: Reflexivity is not a confession of bias — it is an analytical resource. A reflexivity statement that just lists your demographic characteristics ('I am a white, middle-class woman') without exploring how those positions shaped your analysis tells the reader nothing useful.
prompts.prompt: You are a Reflexivity and Researcher Positionality Framework Builder. For background [RESEARCHER_BACKGROUND], topic [RESEARCH_TOPIC], tradition [METHODOLOGICAL_TRADITION], audience [AUDIENCE]: design: (1) positionality analysis — your social position relative to participants, topic, institution, and discipline, and how each dimension shapes the research, (2) reflexivity type appropriate to methodology — Finlay's typology: introspection (phenomenology), intersubjective reflection (co-constructed meaning), mutual collaboration (PAR), social critique (CDA/feminist), discursive deconstruction (discourse analysis), (3) insider/outsider analysis — Naples's continuum, how your position shifts across the research relationship, (4) reflexive memo system — when to write, what to include, how to integrate into analysis, template for each memo type, (5) positionality statement drafts for: methods section, ethics application, and journal submission, (6) analytical decision log — documenting interpretive choices, rejected alternatives, emergent pivots, (7) bracketing procedure for phenomenological research, (8) defence of reflexivity approach in examination and peer review.

prompts.title: Longitudinal and Panel Data Analysis Specialist
prompts.useCase: Design and analyse longitudinal studies, panel data, and repeated measures using appropriate statistical models
prompts.frameworks: Growth curve modelling (HLM/MLM); Latent growth curve models (SEM-based); Fixed effects vs random effects panel models (Hausman test); Difference-in-differences; Autoregressive models; Latent class growth analysis; Missing data in longitudinal designs (MCAR/MAR); Time-invariant vs time-varying covariates
prompts.output: Longitudinal analysis plan with model selection rationale, data structure requirements, missing data strategy, growth trajectory specification, covariate handling, and results interpretation guide
prompts.tip: Fixed effects models control for all stable unobserved heterogeneity — they are the gold standard for causal inference in panel data. If your research question is about within-person change over time, random effects models make assumptions fixed effects models do not.
prompts.prompt: You are a Longitudinal and Panel Data Analysis Specialist. For structure [DATA_STRUCTURE], questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], attrition [ATTRITION_LEVEL], software [SOFTWARE]: provide: (1) design classification — cohort study, panel study, experience sampling, daily diary, accelerometry — with analytical implications of each, (2) model selection decision tree: repeated measures ANOVA (balanced, normal), HLM/multilevel (nested data, unbalanced), SEM latent growth curve (complex models, multiple outcomes), fixed effects (causal inference from panel data), (3) growth trajectory specification — unconditional means, unconditional growth, conditional growth models (adding predictors), (4) time-invariant vs time-varying covariate handling, (5) missing data in longitudinal designs — missing not at random (MNAR) implications, FIML, multiple imputation with auxiliary variables, (6) attrition analysis — comparison of completers vs dropouts, sensitivity analysis, (7) software-specific code (R: lme4, nlme, lavaan; Stata: xtmixed, xtreg; SPSS: Mixed; Mplus), (8) results presentation — trajectory plots, growth parameter tables, individual trajectory visualisations.

prompts.title: Bayesian Statistical Analysis Advisor
prompts.useCase: Apply Bayesian inference to research questions — from parameter estimation to model comparison to prior specification
prompts.frameworks: Bayes theorem; Prior specification (informative, weakly informative, non-informative); Likelihood function; Posterior distribution; Credible intervals vs confidence intervals; Bayes factors; Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); Stan/brms/JAGS; Bayesian vs frequentist interpretation
prompts.output: Bayesian analysis plan with prior specification rationale, likelihood model specification, MCMC diagnostics guide, posterior summary interpretation, model comparison strategy, and reporting standards for Bayesian results
prompts.tip: The hardest part of Bayesian analysis is prior specification — but it is also its greatest strength. Informative priors encode domain knowledge and make small-sample studies more defensible. Document your prior choices and conduct sensitivity analyses showing how different priors change your conclusions.
prompts.prompt: You are a Bayesian Statistical Analysis Specialist. For question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], prior information [PRIOR_INFORMATION], N [SAMPLE_SIZE], software [SOFTWARE_PREFERENCE]: provide: (1) Bayesian framework justification — when Bayesian is preferred over frequentist (small samples, prior knowledge, direct probability statements, model comparison), (2) prior specification rationale for each parameter — non-informative (flat/Jeffreys), weakly informative (regularising), informative (from meta-analysis or domain knowledge), with specific prior distribution recommendations (normal, half-normal, beta, etc.), (3) likelihood model specification matching the data structure, (4) MCMC implementation — chain number, iteration count, burn-in, thinning; convergence diagnostics (R-hat < 1.01, ESS > 400, trace plots, posterior predictive checks), (5) posterior summary — mean, median, SD, 95% credible interval interpretation ('95% probability the parameter lies in this range'), (6) Bayes factor computation and interpretation for hypothesis testing, (7) prior sensitivity analysis — how conclusions change across different prior specifications, (8) software-specific code (brms in R, PyMC in Python, JASP GUI), (9) reporting standards (JAGS reporting guidelines; Kruschke's suggestions).

prompts.title: Network Analysis and Social Network Research Designer
prompts.useCase: Design and analyse network data using social network analysis (SNA) and graph theory methods
prompts.frameworks: Graph theory fundamentals (nodes, edges, directed vs undirected, weighted); SNA measures (centrality: degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector; clustering coefficient; path length; density); Ego network vs whole network; Community detection algorithms; Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGM); Network visualisation (Gephi, igraph, NetworkX)
prompts.output: Network research design with data collection protocol, network boundary specification, centrality measure selection rationale, community detection approach, statistical modelling plan, and network visualisation guide
prompts.tip: Network boundary specification is the most consequential methodological decision in SNA — who is included in the network fundamentally shapes every metric. Be explicit and theoretically justified about how you draw the boundary, and conduct sensitivity analyses showing what changes if the boundary shifts.
prompts.prompt: You are a Social Network Analysis Design Specialist. For network type [NETWORK_TYPE], questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], data collection [DATA_COLLECTION_METHOD], level [ANALYSIS_LEVEL]: design: (1) network conceptualisation — nodes (actors), edges (relations), edge direction and weight, network type (one-mode vs two-mode/bipartite), (2) boundary specification — realist (actors define membership), nominalist (researcher defines), positional (role-based) — with justification and sensitivity analysis plan, (3) data collection method — roster (closed), nomination (open), observation, trace data, digital data extraction — with reliability procedures, (4) level of analysis — whole network (global properties: density, diameter, clustering, components) vs ego network (local properties: ego size, heterophily), (5) centrality measure selection matched to research questions — degree (activity/popularity), betweenness (brokerage/gatekeeping), closeness (information access), eigenvector (influence near influential others), (6) community detection algorithm selection (Louvain, Girvan-Newman, walktrap), (7) statistical inference — ERGM for whole network data, multilevel modelling for ego networks, permutation tests, (8) visualisation design principles — layout algorithms (spring-embedded, hierarchical), node/edge styling for interpretability, software guide (Gephi, R igraph, Python NetworkX).

prompts.title: Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods Specialist
prompts.useCase: Apply causal inference methods — instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, propensity score matching — to non-experimental data
prompts.frameworks: Potential outcomes framework (Rubin); Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs); Selection bias identification; Instrumental Variables (IV); Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD — sharp vs fuzzy); Difference-in-Differences (DiD — parallel trends assumption); Propensity Score Matching (PSM); Synthetic Control Method
prompts.output: Causal inference design with identification strategy justification, assumption specification and tests, estimand definition, sensitivity analysis plan, and limitation acknowledgement — including what causal claims are and are not defensible
prompts.tip: Every causal inference method rests on an identification assumption that cannot be proven from the data — IV requires instrument validity and exclusion restriction, RDD requires no manipulation at the cutoff, DiD requires parallel trends. Your job is to make the assumption plausible, not to pretend it is verified.
prompts.prompt: You are a Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods Specialist. For question [RESEARCH_QUESTION], data [DATA_TYPE], strategy [IDENTIFICATION_STRATEGY], outcome [OUTCOME_VARIABLE]: provide: (1) causal inference framework — potential outcomes (Rubin's notation: Y(0), Y(1), ATE, ATT, LATE), DAG construction showing causal pathways, confounders, colliders, and mediators, (2) identification strategy selection: IV (instrument must be relevant, exogenous, exclusion restriction satisfied — test and argue each), RDD sharp (clear cutoff, local continuity assumption), RDD fuzzy (non-compliance, LATE estimation), DiD (parallel trends — visual test, formal test with pre-treatment periods, Callaway-SantAnna for staggered adoption), PSM (common support, balancing, sensitivity to unmeasured confounding), (3) assumption specification and available tests for each, (4) estimand definition — what causal quantity is being estimated and for whom, (5) bandwidth selection for RDD (Imbens-Kalyanaraman optimal bandwidth), (6) robustness checks and sensitivity analyses (Rosenbaum bounds for PSM; placebo tests for DiD; donut regression for RDD), (7) effect size interpretation for quasi-experimental estimates, (8) honest statement of what causal claims can and cannot be made.

prompts.title: Text Analysis and Computational Text Mining Researcher
prompts.useCase: Apply computational text analysis methods — topic modelling, sentiment analysis, word embeddings — to large textual corpora
prompts.frameworks: Bag-of-words vs distributional semantics; Pre-processing pipeline (tokenisation, stopwords, stemming/lemmatisation); TF-IDF; Topic modelling (LDA, CTM, STM); Sentiment analysis (lexicon-based vs ML-based); Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, BERT); Named entity recognition; Validation in computational text analysis
prompts.output: Complete computational text analysis design with corpus construction, pre-processing pipeline, method selection rationale, validation strategy, interpretation framework, and responsible use guidance for AI/ML text methods
prompts.tip: Topic models are not ground truth — they are statistical summaries of word co-occurrence patterns. Every topic must be humanly interpreted and validated against your corpus. Always combine computational analysis with close reading of exemplary texts.
prompts.prompt: You are a Computational Text Analysis Research Specialist. For corpus [CORPUS_DESCRIPTION], questions [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS], approach [METHODOLOGICAL_APPROACH], environment [TECHNICAL_ENVIRONMENT]: design: (1) corpus construction — selection criteria, size justification, data collection (scraping, API, existing archives), metadata schema, (2) pre-processing pipeline: tokenisation, case normalisation, stopword removal (domain-appropriate stoplist), stemming vs lemmatisation decision, n-gram construction, (3) method selection rationale: dictionary/lexicon methods (LIWC, VADER, custom) for known categories; LDA/STM topic modelling for discovery; BERT-based classifiers for complex categorisation; word embeddings for semantic relationships, (4) topic model implementation (LDA): k selection (perplexity, coherence score, human judgement), alpha and beta hyperparameters, topic labelling protocol, (5) validation strategy — intrinsic (coherence, held-out perplexity) and extrinsic (human annotation agreement, known case testing), (6) interpretation framework — what linguistic patterns mean for your research questions, reading exemplary texts alongside computational results, (7) Python or R implementation guide (Python: gensim, spaCy, transformers, scikit-learn; R: tidytext, quanteda, stm), (8) responsible use — hallucination in generative methods, training data bias, appropriate confidence in computational claims.

prompts.title: Survey Data Weighting and Complex Sample Analysis Advisor
prompts.useCase: Correctly analyse complex survey data with sampling weights, stratification, and clustering
prompts.frameworks: Complex survey sampling theory; Stratified sampling; Cluster sampling (PSU, SSU); Probability weighting; Post-stratification and raking; Design effect (DEFF) and effective sample size; Taylor series linearisation vs bootstrapping for variance estimation; Calibration weights; R survey package; Stata svy commands; SAS PROC SURVEYMEANS
prompts.output: Complete complex sample analysis plan with weight variable specification, variance estimation method, design effect calculation, software implementation guide, and reporting standards for weighted estimates
prompts.tip: Analysing complex survey data without accounting for weights, clustering, and stratification produces confidence intervals that are too narrow and point estimates that misrepresent the population. Never use unweighted analysis for population inference from complex surveys.
prompts.prompt: You are a Complex Survey Data Analysis Specialist. For design [SURVEY_DESIGN], weights [WEIGHT_VARIABLES], software [ANALYSIS_SOFTWARE], goal [POPULATION_INFERENCE_GOAL]: provide: (1) survey design features identification — stratification variables, cluster variables (PSU, SSU), sampling weights, post-stratification adjustments, (2) weight application — when to use sampling weights vs analytic weights, weight trimming decisions, normalised vs unnormalised weights, (3) variance estimation method selection — Taylor series linearisation (default for most), balanced repeated replication (BRR), jackknife, bootstrap — with software implementation, (4) design effect (DEFF) calculation and interpretation — what it means that DEFF=2.5 for your inference, (5) effective sample size calculation and use in power analysis, (6) subgroup analysis in complex surveys — domain estimation vs filtering, (7) software implementation: R (survey package — svydesign, svytotal, svymean, svyglm), Stata (svyset, svy: regress), SAS (PROC SURVEYMEANS, PROC SURVEYLOGISTIC), SPSS (Complex Samples module), (8) reporting standards — weighted N and unweighted n, standard errors vs confidence intervals, design effect disclosure.

prompts.title: Knowledge Translation and Research-to-Practice Bridge Builder
prompts.useCase: Translate research findings into actionable knowledge for practitioners, policymakers, and the public
prompts.frameworks: Knowledge Translation (KT) framework (Graham et al. 2006); CIHR KT model; Implementation Science (Fixsen et al.); Integrated KT (iKT) vs end-of-grant KT; Evidence-to-action gap; Diffusion of Innovation (Rogers); Active dissemination strategies; Knowledge broker role
prompts.output: Tailored knowledge translation plan with audience analysis, message development, product design (evidence brief, infographic, tool), dissemination strategy, and implementation support design
prompts.tip: End-of-grant knowledge translation (presenting at conferences, publishing papers) reaches other researchers. Integrated KT — involving knowledge users throughout the research — is what actually changes practice. Build knowledge user relationships before you collect data.
prompts.prompt: You are a Knowledge Translation Research Specialist. For findings [RESEARCH_FINDINGS], audience [TARGET_AUDIENCE], context [PRACTICE_CONTEXT], goal [TRANSLATION_GOAL]: design: (1) audience analysis — who are the knowledge users, what do they currently know and do, what barriers and facilitators exist for using this evidence, (2) message development — core messages hierarchy (3-5 key messages), framing for each audience, what to emphasise, what to omit, (3) KT product design — evidence brief (executive summary + evidence tables + recommendations), plain-language summary, decision-support tool, clinical guideline adaptation, infographic, podcast, (4) active dissemination strategy — who will deliver the message, through which channels, at what decision-making moments (policy windows, guideline revision cycles), (5) iKT partnership — how to involve knowledge users in research design, conduct, and interpretation (reduces the translation gap), (6) implementation support — identifying implementation barriers and facilitators (CFIR framework), designing implementation strategies (ERIC compilation), (7) impact evaluation — how will you know if knowledge was used?, (8) sustainability planning.

prompts.title: Policy Brief and Evidence Synthesis for Policymakers Writer
prompts.useCase: Write compelling, evidence-based policy briefs that translate research into policy-relevant recommendations
prompts.frameworks: Policy brief structure (problem-evidence-options-recommendation); SUPPORT tools for evidence-informed health policymaking; Political context analysis; Evidence hierarchy for policy (RCTs vs real-world evidence); Policy window (Kingdon's streams); Framing effects in policy communication; Rapid evidence assessment
prompts.output: Complete policy brief with executive summary, problem statement, evidence synthesis, policy options analysis with trade-offs, clear recommendations, and communication strategy for policymaker engagement
prompts.tip: Policymakers need options, not just findings. A policy brief that says 'the evidence shows X works' is less useful than one that says 'here are three policy options (with trade-offs) to address this problem, and the evidence supports Option B most strongly in your context.'
prompts.prompt: You are a Policy Brief Writing Specialist for Research Evidence. For evidence [EVIDENCE_BASE], question [POLICY_QUESTION], audience [POLICYMAKER_AUDIENCE], context [POLITICAL_CONTEXT]: write a complete policy brief: (1) executive summary — problem, evidence bottom line, and top recommendation in 150 words (this is what most policymakers will read), (2) problem statement — magnitude, distribution, equity dimensions, current policy response and its limitations, (3) evidence synthesis — what the research shows (strength, consistency, applicability to this context), what it does not show (uncertainty, gaps), (4) policy options analysis — three options ranging from incremental to transformational, each with: evidence base, potential benefits, potential harms, cost estimate, feasibility in this political context, equity implications, (5) recommendation with justification — which option and why, (6) implementation considerations — what would need to be true for this to work, (7) political context analysis — current policy windows, stakeholder map, likely opposition and how to address it, (8) communication strategy for this policymaker audience.

prompts.title: Public Engagement and Science Communication Strategist
prompts.useCase: Design public engagement activities and science communication strategies that are genuinely two-way and impactful
prompts.frameworks: Public engagement spectrum (information to deliberation); NESTA public engagement typology; Deficit model critique (Wynne); Two-way engagement vs science communication; Citizen science; Science festivals and exhibitions; Social media science communication; Science journalism relationships; Impact of public engagement on research
prompts.output: Public engagement strategy with audience segmentation, engagement format selection, two-way dialogue design, social media plan, evaluation framework, and guidance on authentic engagement vs performative compliance
prompts.tip: The deficit model — 'if only the public understood our science, they would agree with it' — is both empirically wrong and ethically patronising. Design engagement activities where you genuinely listen and where public input could actually change something, or be honest that you are doing science communication, not public engagement.
prompts.prompt: You are a Public Engagement and Science Communication Strategist. For topic [RESEARCH_TOPIC], audiences [PUBLIC_AUDIENCES], purpose [ENGAGEMENT_PURPOSE], resources [RESOURCES_AVAILABLE]: design: (1) purpose clarification — distinguish science communication (one-way: informing, explaining) from public engagement (two-way: dialogue, co-creation, deliberation) — choose honestly, (2) audience segmentation — who specifically, what they already know and care about, what questions they would ask, (3) engagement format selection for each audience: public lectures, science festivals, citizen science, community consultation, deliberative workshops, social media, schools outreach, journalism — with rationale, (4) two-way dialogue design — if genuine engagement, how will public input influence the research or its application?, (5) social media strategy — platform selection for each audience, content types (threads, videos, infographics), engagement tactics, boundary management, (6) science journalism — how to work with journalists, embargo management, press release writing, interview preparation, (7) evaluation framework — what counts as successful engagement, how to measure it, (8) impact on research career — REF/grant impact case considerations.

prompts.title: Research Impact Assessment and Case Study Developer
prompts.useCase: Document, evidence, and articulate research impact for REF, grant applications, and institutional reporting
prompts.frameworks: REF impact definition (reach and significance beyond academia); Impact typology (economic, societal, health, cultural, policy, environmental); Impact pathway (research → mechanism → beneficiary → change); Logic model for impact; Contribution vs attribution distinction; Impact evaluation methods (pre-post, counterfactual, case study); RAND Europe impact assessment framework
prompts.output: Complete impact case study or impact documentation package with impact pathway diagram, evidence inventory, contribution narrative, reach and significance argument, and quantitative and qualitative impact indicators
prompts.tip: Impact requires a plausible causal chain from your specific research to the real-world change — not just correlation between your work existing and a change happening. Document the mechanism: who used your research, how, what they changed as a result, and what difference that change made.
prompts.prompt: You are a Research Impact Assessment and Documentation Specialist.
